**Lightning shielding: its own user-guide page, and what its review
found** (owner: "lightning shielding needs a link to its own page too").
The window gets the check pages' treatment
([check pages](check-pages.md) §6): its own page
([Lightning shielding](../user-guide/lightning-shielding.md)), opened by
the **user guide ↗** buttons of *1 What it checks*, *2 Scope*, *3 Rules*
and the Results; the grey lines between the fields moved into the
section's (?) and the fields' hovers (each saying what it changes in the
result). No *Model* section: every modelling setting (the calculations,
the step) belongs to a rule, so that a preset brings it. Found while
writing the page:

- **Fixed (a clear fault, not on the safe side): the inner angle beyond
  the outer shielding wire.** A phase took a shielding wire's inner
  angle whenever another shielding wire lay on its side of that wire,
  however far: a phase *outside* the outer shielding wire, beyond that
  wire's outer line, could be said covered by the inner angle of the
  wire farther away (e.g. wires at different heights, the inner angle
  larger than the outer), while the covered zone drawn showed it
  outside. Now the inner angle applies only to a phase **between** the
  wire and another shielding wire across the cut — the classical
  reading, and what the drawing showed. Results change only for such
  phases, towards exposed; the example and the benchmarks
  (`electrical-064`, `-065`) are unchanged.
- **Said (not on the safe side): the step.** Each cross-section stands
  for its step: an exposure shorter than a step, between two cuts or
  within half a step of a structure, can be missed. Every result (the
  window and `ohl lightning`) now says *NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE: each
  cross-section stands for its step …*; the method is unchanged.
- **Said: no terrain loaded.** The ground straight between the
  structures' feet and level across was noted; the note and the
  window's warning now say *NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE* (the theory already
  said so).
- **Said (presentation): the cross-section drawn.** Only the last rule
  × case pair's cuts are kept; a row of another pair drew that pair's
  cut (its colours that pair's verdict), said only with several rules.
  Now said whenever the row is not of the pair drawn.
- **Marked conservative in the theory:** every free sphere centre
  counts, also one in a pocket under the shielding wires that a sphere
  from above could not reach.

**Load cases made simple: groups of structures, the library cases only**
(owner: "in line criteria loads for structure there's an old part for the
load cases that makes no sense to have anymore. also the loadcase library
and loadcases per structure type should be moved to structures and maybe
reworked in this new concept. i was a bit confused on how to do things so
please make them simpler and more understandable. i think most of the
features here are doubled with simply defining load cases and then have
them attributed in groups of pylons"; the plan of 2026-11-14 approved
with "go ahead with your recommendations"). Built, in active development,
not approved yet:

- **Line › Criteria › Loads for structures is gone.** A placed structure
  gets its library cases only (their unfactored values per quantity and
  their factors), in OHL-Structure as before; an extra load case there
  takes the unfactored forces of any of them, broken-wire cases included.
  The weather cases once sent unfactored, the wires' condition for them
  and the broken-wire cases sent (`structure_loads.weather_cases`,
  `condition`, `broken_cases`, and the older `load_cases`) are read, kept
  and no longer used; one note says so (`Line::unused_structure_loads_note`,
  in the groups window and in Checks › Structure loads). With them goes
  the second body-wind rule: a library case takes the member wind (drag
  and shielding) — one rule. The line-values file keeps its format and
  version (8): no new field, `weather_case` sources only in older files.
  An older file's weather cases still run in OHL-Structure, said **NOT ON
  THE SAFE SIDE** (every factor 1, body wind without drag or shielding);
  an extra case naming a line case not sent gets no value and is said
  **NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE** in the status block, never run silently.
- **The load case library and the groups are in Line › Structures**:
  *Load cases…* (the library, the same form) and *Load cases per group…*
  (a new window on the check pages' guidelines: numbered sections with
  (?) help and a user guide page of its own, every change one command).
- **Groups only.** A structure takes the union of the cases of the groups
  it is in (two groups: both, the safe side); in no group, every case; in
  groups ticking none only, none (the former *takes no load case*). No
  own set per structure and no set per type any more: a structure's
  Properties shows its groups and cases only. Membership: structures
  picked by hand (*Add the N selected*, from the Structures table or a
  view) and/or rules, all of which must hold — types, line angle from–to
  (degrees), station from–to on an alignment, dead end yes/no read from
  the line — live as the line is edited; the usage notes and
  OHL-Structure's status block say which groups a structure is in.
- **Formats.** Line file version **18** for `structure_groups`, written
  only by a line with one (`BEFORE_GROUPS_VERSION` 17); OHL XML
  `<structure_group>` (`docs/schema/ohl-line.xsd`); project `meta` row
  `structure_groups` (`Session::structure_groups_command`). Older lines
  are read into groups (`Line::adopt_structure_groups`): a group `type X`
  per type set (rule type X), a group per distinct own set (picking its
  structures, named after them), a group `no load case` for the structures
  that took none; each description says where it came from; an older
  project is rewritten so once when it opens.

**To confirm** (chosen on the safe side or the simplest, not asked):
1. *Older sets read with the union.* A structure that had its own set and
   whose type had a set now takes both; one that took *none* and whose
   type had a set now takes its type's cases. More cases (the safe side),
   but not exactly the old result; the guide asks to look at *7 Who is in*
   after opening an older project.
2. *Line angle rule:* the size of the angle (left or right), the largest
   over the alignments whose run the structure is on; a structure on no
   alignment's run has none and is not taken by an angle rule (it then
   takes its other groups', or every case in none).
3. *Dead end:* a section of the line ends at the structure (its first or
   last point); a string flagged strain alone does not count.
4. *Older line-values files* holding weather cases sent on their own are
   still run, said NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE, rather than refused: they are
   rewritten when the structure is opened from OHL-Design again.
5. *A deleted structure* stays in the groups that picked it (shown *(not
   in the line)*, left out); a renamed one follows.
6. Rules on the height and the ground elevation (in the plan of
   2026-11-14) are not built: the owner's list named types, angle,
   station and dead end.

**Ice on the structures from the wires' ice, with a factor** (owner: "for
the ice on the load cases can you also add a factor as for the wind to
change the value compared to the conductor weather cases"; asked which
factor, the owner chose a factor on the conductor ice): load case file
version 6 — `[case.structure] ice = "weather"` puts the weather case's
ice thickness on the wires on every structure taking the case (density:
the case's, the weather case's, else glaze ice as on the wires; a weather
case giving its ice as a load per metre is refused there — no thickness
made up), and `ice_factor` multiplies the structures' ice thickness
whichever its source (the wires', the local, one given). The weight then
takes the vertical factor as before. A factor below 1 is the engineer's
choice, not judged. The Load cases library form: *the wires' ice* and
*factor on the thickness*; its first choice *by the weather case* renamed
*default* (it never took the weather case's ice). Written at 6 only when a
case uses either.

**Post insulators on structure types, drawn in OHL-Structure** (the post
plan's phase 2c, steps 2 and 3; owner, 2026-11-14: "the post insulator
might be needed on pylons too", "decide if its base is hinged or not"): a
structure type's string can be a post with every field of a line's post —
`post`, `hinged`, `cantilever_load`, `exit_angle`, `exit_direction`
(units in the values, as the type's `angle` and `direction`; the line's
`exit_angle_deg`, `exit_direction_deg`) — structure file version 13,
written only when a string gives one. Resolving the line carries them into
its strings, so a typed post loads, is checked and sends its moment to
OHL-Structure exactly as one made by hand (the tests compare both). The
type is refused where the line refuses the strings (a fixed post sharing
its wire point, a hinged one without a brace, a strain post, a post on a
wire point, a post's field on a plain string). OHL-Structure's Strings
table has a **post** column (none, fixed, hinged; its rating and its
clamp's exit angle and direction), each change one undo step, a change
that would make a post invalid refused before the file changes; the 3D
view draws a post thick from its base to its wire point, a fixed post's
base plate or a hinged post's hinge, and its clamp's exit direction where
given. A string saved to the insulator library from OHL-Structure is a
library post when it is a post. **Fault fixed on the way**: OHL-Design's
structure editor (a structure without a type, *Strings and points…*)
dropped a post's fields — its Apply made a post an ordinary string, and
*Make it a type…* wrote it so; it now keeps them. **Choices made, to
confirm** (nothing here is less safe than before): a post's `angle`
defaults to 0 (hanging) as for any string, so an upright post needs
`angle = "180 deg"` (no hidden default); the exit-angle keys are
`exit_angle` / `exit_direction` (the `.ohls` convention of units in the
values) rather than the line's `…_deg` names; a hinged post is made in
OHL-Structure after its brace (a hinged post without one is refused, as
in the line). **Found, to confirm**: a hinged post with one brace whose
base is straight above the post's (the shape of the *braced* preset)
turns freely along the line, both members being pinned; with unbalanced
pulls the section's rolling does not settle and the section is reported
not solved (its loads missing, said — nothing unsafe is computed). How
pivoting line posts are to be modelled is the owner's question; two
braces hold it (*answered the same day: [a pivoting post is held by what
is attached to it](#2026-11-15), above*). Not yet: posts on the type in OHL-Design's type workspace
table (they are kept there, not shown as a column), a post's ratings
shown in OHL-Structure.

## 2026-11-14

**Post insulators on pylons in OHL-Structure** (owner: "the post
insulator might be needed on pylons too"; "decide if its base is hinged or
not to have moments or not transmitted to the pylon keeping the unsafe
warnings if a moment is transmitted into a truss"): the line sends a fixed
post's moment to OHL-Structure split by force component (line-values file
version 8), its load cases factor it exactly, the finite-element check
applies it where a frame meets the joint and says NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE
where only trusses meet (the pole check too); a hinged post sends forces
only. Fault fixed: the values at a post's base were sent twice and only the
first read — now summed per point. Next: a type's strings as posts with
every field; posts drawn in OHL-Structure.

**Post insulators, fourth step: posts on the ground** (the post plan's
phase 4): Add post insulator clicked on the ground, or the tick in Add
structure for a new structure without a type, makes a **post support** —
a point on top of a pedestal (2.5 m), an upright post on it (1.5 m) and
its wire point with a set — in one step. The pedestal is a point: its own
weight and wind are not in the loads, said NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE for its
foundation; a pedestal structure type (OHL-Structure) is left for later.

**Post insulators, third step: the Add post insulator tool** (the post
plan's phase 3; owner: "go ahead for the rest" — of the posts): a tool of
the Structures theme (its icon `add-post.svg`), and on the right-click
menu of a structure or a point; the strings window's shapes *upright*,
*horizontal* and *braced* post (1.5 m to start from); every string's
post fields in the window (post, hinged, cantilever rating, exit angle and
direction, compression and tension ratings) — before, Apply on a post in
the strings window made it an ordinary string again (a fault of the
first step, fixed). A post's window says *stands on*, shows no swing
limits. The limits' help no longer says they are not checked (the string
check checks them since 2026-10-24).

**Local conditions reach OHL-Structure** (phase 1c of the load cases
review, owner's answer 3): Checks › Structure loads › Use local
conditions is kept with the project (project setting
`app.structure_loads.<line>`, as the other check windows keep theirs:
no line file change), and the loads written for a placed structure
take it — every library case and every line result as if it said
`use_local = true` (`StructureCases::with_local`), the same loads as the
line's check; OHL-Structure's status block says "With the local
conditions". Before, they were computed as written whatever the switch:
lower than the line check's at a structure with `wind_static` above 1,
**not on the safe side**, not said. Changing the switch rewrites the
open structures' line values. The line results take it too (one rule:
the switch means every case takes the local conditions).

**One name, one meaning** (phase 1b of the load cases review, owner's
answers 4 and 7): a weather case sent to the structures (Loads for
structures) with the name of a load case of the library is sent as
`<name> (weather case)` and said in OHL-Structure's status block;
before, both arrived as `everyday`, OHL-Structure took the first (the
library's) for both, and an extra case built on the weather case got the
library case's forces — its wire condition, removed or broken wires,
local conditions — **not on the safe side**, without a word. An extra
case still naming `everyday` in its line forces gets the library case's
and the status block says so. Typed values that land on no row (their
case renamed or gone since) are **not run** (before, a case of their
own while the real case ran without them: not on the safe side): the
Load table lists them with Move (to the case they belong to), Make it a
load case (a case holding only typed values, e.g. a client's load tree)
and Take back. Found on the way: the line results were solved with the
weather cases sent only, so a line result after creep failed when the
creep-stretch case itself was not sent (its values missing, said in the
note); the line's own weather cases now go along.

**Never silently absent: renamed or deleted load cases, a faulty case**
(phase 1a of the load cases review, owner's answers 5 and 6): a structure
whose case set names cases not in the load case library is **not
checked** — said in every case's notes, in the usage (never a pass; a set
naming only such cases is listed in every case with no loads), in the
Structures table (⚠, error colour) and in OHL-Structure's header; before,
it quietly took fewer cases, or none and dropped out of the usage table
(**not on the safe side**). The sets are checked against the whole
library, not the cases ticked in the check (a run of some cases no
longer calls the others "not in the library"). **Rename** in the Load
cases library renames the case in the file (comments kept) and in every
structure's set, type's set and broken-wire tick, one command undone as
one (`load_case_sets::rename_command`); **Delete** names the structures
that lose it. A library case that does not compute fails only itself in
what OHL-Structure gets (`ohl_loads::structure_loads_each`): the others
are sent, the faulty one is named NOT SENT in the header of the
structures taking it; before, one faulty case removed every library case
of every structure. The line's own check still stops at a faulty case
and says why (visible, nothing passes).

**Load cases between OHL-Design and OHL-Structure: the model, and the
texts said right** (owner, approving the review of how load cases reach
the structures, with its recommended answers): *the line transfers what
the wires do* — forces per load case, per wire set, back and ahead —
*the structure side decides what acts* (factors, the cases it takes,
back and ahead shares, points left out) *and checks it*; construction
stages are load cases of OHL-Structure (a reduced tension set on the
line side is dropped from the plan). Phase 0: a user-guide page [How
load cases reach a structure](../user-guide/load-cases-to-structures.md)
(the words once, the flow as a picture, each window, where the factors
are applied, the order own set ► type's set ► every case); the texts
that still said the line's load cases are "no longer sent" or that the
line gives "forces, nothing else" corrected (Loads for structures, the
structure load cases' flow, the spec's status, OHL-Structure's start
for a placed structure, code comments); the Loads for structures menu
says, with no weather case ticked, that the library cases still arrive;
OHL-Structure's "the project has no load cases" now shows when the line
has no load case library and sends no weather case (the line's message
began with other words: `ohl_structure_loads::NO_LOAD_CASE_FILE`).

**Field cuts and steps fail on their own** (owner: on a real line the 2D
cuts at buildings "failed because of one unconnected cable and all
results got aborted … for cuts those that work get their results reported
and those that fail get an error"): in the magnetic and electric fields
each cut is computed on its own and a failed one is listed in a NOT
COMPUTED note with why; the windows keep the steps that worked (profiles,
cuts, volumes) when another fails; Stop still ends the run. Notes
beginning NOT COMPUTED are drawn in the error colour, NOT ON THE SAFE
SIDE in the warning colour, in both field windows.

**Staking table** (owner: "can you go ahead and make a staking table",
after the gap list against the established line-design program named a
staking report as missing; then "it would be better to have it under
structure"): Line › Structures › Staking table… and `ohl
staking` (`ohl_line::staking`) — per structure and alignment its station,
offset, line angle, back and ahead span, coordinates, ground and the
difference, height adjustment and the bearing of its ahead axis; per foot
of a typed structure modelled to its feet (supported joints, the
extension and leg extensions applied) its leg A–D, offset in the
structure's axes, coordinates and its height above the ground. Choices
made without asking (to confirm): bearings from grid north of the line's
CRS; a structure on two alignments listed on each; the feet as the
type's supported joints (guy anchors included, unlabelled); no reference
stakes, foundation sizes or excavation ([Staking
table](../user-guide/staking-table.md)).

**Post insulators, second step** (owner: "go ahead with the next
steps"):

1. **A jumper's load on a clamp fixed to the structure** (a post's top,
   a wire point without strings) goes into that clamp's force on the
   structure; before, it was left out — **not on the safe side**, and a
   fault for every wire clamped to a structure with a jumper on it, not
   only posts. And a jumper end where no section ends (a jumper from a
   dead end to a post's top) is loaded in the structure loads like a
   riser's (the estimate, or its own pull, as the line says); before,
   only risers' were.
2. **The jumper's moment on a post's clamp** (`JumperShape::end_moments`,
   from the rod's clamped end) is added to the post's base moment — in
   the structure loads (`AttachmentLoad::couple`, factored by the
   largest of the case's factors) and in the post's check. With the
   estimated jumper loads (the default) the forces are the estimate's
   and the moment the rod's: not one state, said NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE
   with the jumpers named; exact: the jumpers' own pull.
3. **The post's ratings checked** in the string check (`load`): its
   cantilever load (its bending moment at its base over its height, its
   own wind and the clamp's moment in), its compression and tension, each
   where given; unfactored against the ratings as given, as the strings'
   maximum load.
4. **The structure loads' CSV** gains three columns at the end: the
   factored moments about each point (a post's lever and clamp moment;
   0 for the other loads).
5. **Braced posts**: a post on a hinged base (`hinged`, line file version
   17 still — the version is not released) is a member of its assembly
   both ways and needs a brace at its wire point.
6. Not yet: posts on the ground, the Add post tool, the rigid conductor
   on posts, a post's deflection.

**Post insulators, first step** (owner: "go ahead with post"; "on the
post the flexible should come in and have a fixed exit angle"; the
plan's open questions taken with defaults, said in the plan: a post is
rigid, posts on structures first, in OHL-Design):

1. The insulator library's `kind = "post"` (version 6) with its height
   and its optional ratings (`cantilever_load`, `compression_load`,
   `max_load`); a line's string `post` (line file version 17), set from
   a library post.
2. **Rigid**: the wire point a post holds is fixed where the post puts it
   (on the safe side for the post's load, not for clearances by up to its
   deflection — said in the theory).
3. **Its load to its base with the moment of its height**
   (`AttachmentLoad::lever`; the structure analysis applies the moment
   at a frame joint, else says NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE), its own weight and
   wind at its middle.
4. **A jumper at its top leaves at a fixed exit angle** (`exit_angle_deg`,
   `exit_direction_deg`, structure axes; default level, towards the
   jumper's other end).
5. Not yet: the ratings checked, braced posts, posts on the ground, the
   Add post tool, the rigid conductor on posts
   ([Post insulators](../theory/post-insulators.md)).

**Wind on rigid jumpers' end forces** (owner: "go ahead with post and
applying wind to jumpers but I thought wind was applied?"). Wind was
applied to every flexible jumper, and the default estimate of a jumper's
load on its clamps carried a rigid jumper's wind too; but a rigid
jumper's own end forces held its weight and ice only, so with *the
jumper's own pull*, and for a rigid jumper on a tap (*the full loop*,
the default), its wind did not reach the wires — not on the safe side.
Its end forces now carry half its weight, ice and wind each, the wind as
on every jumper ([Jumpers](../theory/jumpers.md#rigid-jumpers)). The
rigid piece's own tube section moves to the rigid conductor (post
insulators plan, phase 5).

**Tap and spacer clamps; objects on each subconductor** (owner: "for the
objects on the line, it doesn't by default adapt to the number of
conductors in the bundle … it's important to have the theory explain the
use of a tap clamp vs a spacer clamp and where it can be mounted. As
well it should be a type of object that can be modified in the load
object library" — "for bundles it's more visually but also to have the
option to multiply the weight with a ticked box is nice"):

1. **Tap clamp and spacer clamp are kinds of their own** in the library
   of point and spread loads (`kind = "tap_clamp"`, `"spacer_clamp"`;
   `.ohlload` version 2), made and changed in its table like any type;
   on an object `clamp_for` (line file version 16). A jumper starting on
   a spacer clamp, a spacer ending on a tap clamp and a spacer clamp on
   a jumper point are refused, saying why; a clamp of either use
   (`clamp`, files from before) takes both. Add string gives a bare end
   the project library's spacer clamp (the template's id, else the first
   of that kind).
2. **On a bundle**: a clamp is drawn on every subconductor (a body too
   when ticked); the tick **per subconductor** (`per_subconductor` on a
   body or a clamp) counts its weight, ice and wind once per
   subconductor — the wind on each without shielding, on the safe side;
   the tap and spacer clamp templates come ticked, bodies not.
3. **Theory**: [Objects on the wires](../theory/line-objects.md) — the
   objects, the tap clamp against the spacer clamp and where each may be
   mounted, bundles, the assumptions marked.

**Imports without opening the project again** (owner: "i wonder if it's
necessary to have a restart when lidar data, orthophotos or dxf are
imported. could we avoid it?" — "go ahead"). After a LiDAR import the
point cloud is read again on its own thread as the project's opening
reads it (`model::read_cloud`, split out of `model::load`;
`crate::cloud_reload`), then put in the model in one frame — points,
class counts, class scheme — and handed to the views as an edit of
points is (`lidar_edit::frame`: points drawn again, profile, cuts,
clearances; the ground built again from the ground classes where it
comes from them, by the run that already did so after an edit); the
points' revisions change, so the checks computed from the points show
they are out of date. After an orthophoto or DXF import, or a removal,
the backgrounds are read again (`backgrounds::reload`) and what draws
them drawn again (the plan's tiles, the 3D drawings, the profile, the
cuts, the sheets' preview); what was imported is switched on. The
weather cases solved, the windows, the camera and the selection stay.
Opening the project again stays only for checking out another version.

**Snap marker lag** (owner: "since adding the red dot, the 3d view on
[a real line] is slower"): the click's search made the list of every clickable
piece again at each pointer move (16 ms on a real line) and projected
all of it; the list is now kept per model and culled by boxes — the
same pick, 30 ms → 1.8 ms a move ([performance](performance.md#measuring-benchmark-desktop-application)).

**Four tool behaviours settled, OHL-Structure's tool windows, the tool
pages' guidelines** (owner, answering the open points of the tool window
rework: "1) close it 2) same it should not use tools 3) not an editing
tool. Viewer can use it 4) removes anything hanging of it 5) go ahead
with structure next. Also write this in the design as for the checks
pages, how the tool pages should be"):

1. **Escape on the Point coordinates window closes it** (the point left
   out, the alignment laid out kept); Enter adds the point. The route
   window takes Enter (make it) and Escape (back to the points). While
   either is open, the alignment's own keys wait.
2. **The plan and the profile use no tool**: as built since 2026-11-01 (a
   left-click selects, whatever tool is held); the code's stale comments
   corrected.
3. **Note is not an editing tool; a viewer uses it**: the session lets a
   viewer put, change, delete, undo and redo annotations whose author is
   them, nothing else (`Session::apply`, `undo`, `redo`;
   `annotations::own_only`) — measurements kept by a viewer too.
4. **A span point deleted takes everything hanging on it**: the spacers
   clamped on it and, new, the jumpers tapped on it (with those hanging
   on them), one undo step. Before, such a deletion was refused (a tap
   left on nothing).
5. **OHL-Structure's tool windows** (the inventory, Delete, Edit's *Open
   in the Detail view?*, Add bolt's *New gauge line?*, Continuous
   members) have the same shape, Escape closes them first; its strips a
   User guide button; the Detail view's tools got sections of their own
   on its tools page. The shared parts moved to `ohl_ui::tool_window`.
6. **[Tool pages: design guidelines](tool-pages.md)**: how a tool window
   and a tool's section of the user guide are built.

**Tool windows made friendlier, tool pages in the book, the tutorial
with screenshots** (owner: "improve the tutorial with screenshots and
create the tool pages in the book to make it easier to understand what
they do as well as improving the small windows that open from the tools
when something is clicked to make it user friendlier for humans that
don't know the programm … functionality stays the same it's just the
cosmetics and placements that change a bit"). Every window a tool opens
starts with one plain sentence of what it does, a (?) with more and a
**User guide ↗** button to the tool's section; help that was only on
hover got a visible (?); small grey lines under a section went behind a
(?) at its title; one button row at the bottom, the action first,
Cancel last (the rule: [Desktop app conventions](ui.md#tool-windows),
the code `crate::tool_ui`). The Measurements panel's kind of
measurement moved above its value (its buttons covered it). No command,
field, default or result changed; the button labels stayed (Apply,
Cancel…). New pages: [Tools](../user-guide/tools.md) and one per theme
of the inventory, and OHL-Structure's tools; every tool has a section,
checked by a test. The tutorial shows the windows of its steps, made by
the test that does its steps. Before and after pictures of the windows
for the owner: local-data/reviews/tool-windows/.

## 2026-11-13

**Checks › Internal clearances… is an entry, not a submenu** (owner:
"there's an internal clearances sub menu. i think it's not necessary
since there is only one and with the same name. if we need more we'll
redesign this later"). The submenu held one item of the same name and a
short description; the entry opens the window directly and its tooltip
carries the description. Nothing else changes.
**Route plan: the paper chosen automatically, its own route, no link to
the sheets; a user guide page for it and for the profile sheets**
(owner: "in the route plan i would also like to have an optimal selection
of paper for the plan and i don't understand why there is a link to the
sheets in this window. please remove it. also for both the route plan and
the sheets, add a explanation page as for the checks").

- **Paper › Automatic**, the route plan's default: for each route the
  smallest of A4, A3, A2, A1, A0, landscape tried before portrait, that
  holds the whole route on one sheet at the plan's scale; when not even
  A0 does, A0 the way with the fewest sheets
  (`ohl_drawing::plans::map_paper`; the sheets are counted, not drawn, so
  the choice costs no time worth measuring). The result says, per route,
  the paper taken. The fixed papers stay offered. The command line keeps
  its `--page` (not automatic).
- **Route**: each plan window (route, situation, phase) has its own route
  choice, every route by default; the **Profile sheets…** link button,
  there because the plans took the Profile sheets window's route, is
  removed. A phase plan with alignments drawn together reads every route,
  as before. The plan set still takes the Profile sheets window's route.
- **User guide pages** [Route plan](../user-guide/route-plan.md) and
  [Profile sheets](../user-guide/profile-sheets.md), opened by the
  windows' **How it works: user guide ↗**; the situation and phase plan
  and plan set windows open the plans' section of the drawings page.

**The snap point: a red dot where a click would pick, in both
applications** (owner: "I would like to have a highlight of what I'm
clicking on with a transparent red point when I move the mouse that's
dependent on the snap settings and can be a bit outer from the point
where I actually click"). While the pointer moves over a view (OHL-Design:
3D, plan, profile, cross-sections; OHL-Structure: the 3D view), a
semi-transparent red dot with a ring marks the point the click there
would pick: a point candidate itself, the nearest point of a line
candidate as projected; none when nothing is within reach. The dot comes
from the click's own search (`selection::pick_shown_at`, the profile's
`Picker::pick_at`, `ohl_structure_edit::pick_at`: each click now calls
the same function), so the dot and the click cannot disagree, and it
follows Edit › Snap. It is found again only when the pointer moved or the
view, the line or the settings changed. View › Show the snap point
(default on) and View › Snap distance (px) (new; default 14 px, the
radius the 3D view had; the 2D views and OHL-Structure keep their 2 px
less, the first-person crosshair 4 px less) are kept per application.
Painter, colour and settings are shared in `ohl_ui::snap_marker`. Not in
OHL-Structure's Detail view yet.

(open: the most used), 4 Scope, 5 Model (folded: the method and how far

**A plugin removed or installed again asks again for more time or
memory** (owner: "if a plugin that requires more time or memory to work
was accepted. if we uninstall it and reinstall it it should ask again").
What the user allowed is kept per plugin version in the shared plugin
settings; removing a plugin in the plugin manager, or installing it
(again), now forgets it for every version of that plugin
(`ohl_plugins::forget_consents`), in both applications. A plugin folder
copied or deleted by hand is not noticed.

## 2026-11-11

**Completing the code-check plugin interface: decided, not built yet (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner: "you can go ahead". What is decided here is the shape; none
of it is built yet — the interface is as the entry below describes it
(members only, run by OHL-Structure only).

- **One world, optional functions.** A code plugin gives members and
  joints through the same export `member-check`: beside `check-members`,
  a second optional function for the joints (plates, covers and splices,
  fillet welds, the bolt group: the plate's geometry and material, the
  bolts with their strengths and places, the welds, the member forces
  arriving per load case, the edge and end distances; back per plate,
  cover and weld the usage per case, the governing check with its
  clause, notes, not-safe) and a third for the minimum distances the
  bolt tools ask for (hole, end, edge, pitch by bolt and plate data).
  Adding a function to a released interface is not additive for plugins
  built before it, so each comes as its own optional export beside
  `member-check` in that world (as `structure-wind` beside a design
  code), found by name; a plugin without it is not broken.
- **Never another code in its place.** With a plugin as the structure's
  method: joints are checked by its joint function, or reported "NOT
  CHECKED by <plugin>, NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE" when it has none (today
  they are still checked by ASCE 10-97: to be removed with this step);
  the bolt tools say "no minimum distances from <plugin>" when it gives
  none; Member details shows the plugin's capacities.
- **Run everywhere the core methods run**, one call for all load cases
  of a structure: OHL-Structure (today one call per case), `ohl
  structures fe` and the line's structure check (today: every member
  not checked, said). The records' mapping
  (`ohl_structure_link::plugin_check`) then moves to the lowest crate
  that may know both the model and the plugin host, the route the line
  already takes for code plugins; `docs/development/structure-app.md`
  to be updated if a crate rule changes.
- **Poles** (ASCE/SEI 48-19, SIA 263 shafts, SIA 265 wood): carried by a
  further optional export of the same world, not by `check-members` — a
  pole is checked along its height, not per member. Its records, to be
  designed with the move of the pole codes and not now: the shaft as
  sections along the height (shape, dimensions, wall or solid, material
  with its strengths), the foundation level and fixity, per load case
  the resultants at each section (axial, two shears, two moments,
  torsion) and the deflection at the top; back per section the usage per
  case, what governs with its clause, notes, not-safe. The pole check
  stays in the core until then.
- **What still blocks moving ASCE 10-97 and SIA 263:2013 out of the
  core** (2026-11-11, nothing of this list is built):
  1. the joint function and the minimum-distances function above, with
     the example plugin and tests through the real host;
  2. plugin methods run by the CLI and the line's structure check, one
     call for all cases everywhere;
  3. a built-up member's `parts` filled; the core's own remarks
     (crossing members, kept active, eccentric ends) appended to a
     plugin's results; the level 4 `connections` mapping tested through
     a plugin;
  4. Member details and the reports showing a plugin's capacities;
  5. a plugin's settings (national parameters): the design-code plugins'
     parameter files are the mechanism to reuse, not looked at yet;
  6. the two codes' validation benchmarks and theory pages running
     against the plugins;
  7. the pole export (above), for the pole codes only.
- **Proposed order for the move** (to be confirmed by the owner):
  1. finish items 1 to 4;
  2. SIA 263:2013 first — the younger of the two in the core and not the
     default, so a mistake in the move cannot change a default result;
     its benchmarks must give the same numbers through the plugin before
     the core copy is removed;
  3. then ASCE 10-97, the default, the same way;
  4. the plugins live in the repository beside the design codes
     (`plugins/codes/`), built and tested by the full check, and are
     **shipped inside the applications' bundles** and found before the
     user's folder, so a fresh install has them and a tower is never
     left without its default check; a bundled plugin that does not load
     is an error at start, not a silent fallback;
  5. files that name the core methods today (`capacity = "asce10-97"`,
     `"sia263-2013"`, or nothing) keep reading unchanged: those names
     become aliases of the bundled plugins' methods, the default stays
     ASCE 10-97, no file is rewritten and no file version is raised for
     it; `simple` stays in the core.

**A plugin interface for the members' code check (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner: "Go ahead with the interface first once done we'll move the
codes into plugins"; earlier: "maybe the code check should actually be
moved out of the core in plugins that can access the infos they need.
Same as for the rules in the clearances". Built, in active development
(not approved yet).

- **The plan.** First the interface (this entry) with one example
  plugin; then ASCE 10-97 and SIA 263:2013 move out of the core into
  plugins behind it. Until then the two core methods are untouched and
  the default.
- **The interface**: the optional plugin export `member-check`
  (`methods`, `check-members`), additive to interface 0.3; typed records;
  the whole structure in one call — every checked member with its
  section, material, lengths, end conditions, design data, its forces in
  every load case, and its ends' connections only at level 4 with the
  joint details on. Back per member: capacities by name, usage per case,
  what governs, notes, what is not on the safe side. Details:
  [plugins.md](plugins.md#member-checks).
- **Never passing by default.** A member without a result is NOT CHECKED,
  NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE; a file naming a plugin that is not installed is
  refused by name; a program that runs no plugins reports every member
  of such a file as not checked. No other code is ever used in its place.
- **Choosing it**: `[analysis] capacity = "plugin:<plugin>/<method>"`
  (structure file version 12, model file version 5, written at the newer
  version only when used); in OHL-Structure the *capacities* choice lists
  the installed plugins' methods.
- **What still blocks the move of ASCE 10-97 and SIA 263 into plugins**
  (after the completion below; not solved):
  - the two codes themselves are still core code (`asce10.rs`,
    `sia263.rs`, the code branches of `plates.rs` and `bolt_rules.rs`):
    writing them as plugins against the three exports is the move, not
    started; `Analysis::capacity` and `CapacityMethod` stay until then;
  - the interface carries less than the core's own checks read in
    places: the bolt positions of a group are given as lines, pitch,
    span and edge distances (not each bolt's place), a frame member's
    end shear and moments are not in the joint parts (the core's plate
    checks leave them out too, said), and the width of a net section is
    OpenOHL's own choice sent with its words;
  - Member details' live resistance and the reports show no capacities
    of a plugin (the interface returns them —
    `ohl_member_check::Checked::results` —, no run keeps or displays
    them yet: the panel says "resistance: from <plugin> after a run");
  - the joint sheets and the exports were not looked at for values of
    the core's method shown beside a plugin's;
  - the Detail view's bolt tools place freely when the plugin gives no
    minimum distances; only the bolt layout form says so;
  - each plugin call starts the plugin anew (a tower's run: two calls,
    the bolt tools: one per different bolt and part, kept for the
    session) — not measured on a large tower;
  - the pole checks (their own codes): not part of these interfaces;
  - a plugin's own settings (national parameters): not built;
  - the plugins' formulas for the theory pages, and the validation
    benchmarks of the two codes running against the plugins;
  - `tools/check.sh` and the CI workflow do not build
    `plugins/examples/member-check-example` or
    `plugins/tests/member-check-only`: the tests through the host skip
    there (they run where the plugins are built, and fail instead of
    skipping with `OHL_REQUIRE_PLUGIN_TESTS`).
- **Completed the same day** (built, in active development, not
  approved yet): the mapping moved from the link into the core crate
  `ohl-member-check` (it alone knows the finite-element results and the
  plugin host), so that every runner checks alike — OHL-Structure,
  `ohl structures fe` and the line's structure check all run a file's
  plugin method, **one call per structure with all its load cases**; a
  built-up member's `parts` are filled; the core's remarks (kept active,
  a crossing held only by the other diagonal, eccentric ends) are
  appended to the plugin's results. In the line a structure whose plugin
  is not installed fails its check with the message, and members without
  a result count as not on the safe side.
- **Joints and minimum distances** (the same day; built, in active
  development, not approved yet): two more optional exports beside
  `member-check` — a function added to the released interface would
  break the plugins built against it. `joint-check` (every planned part
  of every joint with its force in every case, one call: a member's bolt
  group in a plate or cover with the plate's steel, or a weld) and
  `bolt-distances` (minimum end, spacing and edge distances from the
  bolt and the connected part). With a plugin's method nothing of
  another code is shown: joint rows are the plugin's or read "NOT
  CHECKED by <plugin>, NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE", the bolt tools have the
  plugin's distances or say "no minimum distances from <plugin>", and
  Member details says "resistance: from <plugin> after a run". Details:
  [plugins.md](plugins.md#member-checks).

**Level 4 and the option "joint details in the calculation" (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner: "the structural calculations should be kept on their simpler form with an option to consider the full joint once it's modelled, maybe as a level 4 structure. Without the full joint details it should be level 3". Built, in active development (not approved yet).

- **Level 4** (`Detail::Joints`, "full design with joint details"): a
  level 3 lattice whose every checked member end has its joint detail —
  a `[[connection]]` for that end, or the end running on through the
  joint as one part with a member that says so (`continuous_with`):
  `StructureType::ends_without_joint_details()` is empty. A modelling
  member (`check = false`) and a cable need none. A pole and a structure
  with a separate `model` stay at level 3. Everywhere else level 4
  behaves as level 3. The level is derived, never stored.
- **The option** `joint_details = true`, at the top of the `.ohls`
  (structure file version 11; a file is written at 11 only when it is
  set). Off — the default, also for every existing file: the member
  checks and the finite-element model do not read the connections at
  all (ends from the member's own design data or assumed on the safe
  side, no bolt shear, bearing or net section from connections, no
  `shift` end offsets): exactly the same file without its connections.
  On: as before this decision, and honoured **only at level 4**; set on
  a level 3 file it is not applied and the results say so, with the
  number of ends still without a joint detail.
- **This changes results** of existing files that have connections: they
  are now calculated in the simple form. Intended. The results, the
  report and `ohl structures fe` say which form was used ("members
  checked in the simple form; joint details not taken" / "joint details
  taken").
- **Not on the safe side in every member**: the simple form leaves out a
  connection's bolt shear, bearing and net section and the moment of a
  shifted end, which can govern; it is the form used before the joint
  details existed. Said in the result's note and in the theory pages.
- **Independent of the option**: the joints' own checks (plates, covers,
  welds), Joint details and Member details (the joint's design aid, the
  member shown with its joint details and saying so when the run takes
  the simple form), the drawings and the exports.
- **In OHL-Structure**: a tick *Joint details in the calculation* in
  Results (disabled with the reason below level 4), the header's badge
  *Level 4 — joint details*, and the To do list naming at level 3 what
  level 4 lacks, grouped by joint.
- **The header's count** (UI review the same day): only what blocks a
  calculation counts as "N to do"; on a level 3 structure the header says
  *ready to calculate* and, apart, *optional: level 4, N advice*. The
  "40 to do" of the example tower were 40 advice items (X-braces crossing
  without a joint).

**An internal clearance rule by the system's insulation level (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner: "Insulation level stays in the plugin for the preset but if
it needs to be in the core to apply it to the clearances I would put it
in the core." It is needed in the core for one check: the internal
clearances are run by the core and could not tell a circuit's level, so
a preset had to give the stricter (high) row to every conductor.

- **The condition.** `insulation = "low"` or `"high"` on an
  `[[internal_rule]]`: the rule takes only the parts of the systems of
  that level (`System.insulation_level`; not given on the system: high).
  A rule without it takes every part, exactly as before: no existing
  result changes.
- **How a part's rule is chosen: unchanged.** Every rule whose cases
  and voltages take a part checks it and gives its own row; there was
  and is no precedence ("first" or "largest") among rules. The
  condition is one more filter in the same place.
- **Never skipped silently.** A circuit whose voltage only rules of the
  other level take is said once: "NOT CHECKED, NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE: no
  internal rule for <circuit> (insulation high)". (A voltage that no
  rule names at all is not said today, as before — seen on the way, for
  the owner.)
- **Earth wires** have no system: not parts, as before.
- **Named in the results**: the rule's name with its condition,
  `Phase to steel (insulation low)`, in the rows, the CSV and
  `ohl internal`.
- **Format.** Rule file version 2 only when a rule has the key; older
  files read unchanged.
- **Window.** The internal clearances' rule editor: *any insulation*
  (the default) / *low insulation only* / *high insulation only*, its
  effect on hover; the Systems table's help for *insulation* now names
  this check.
- **Not touched:** the plugin interface; a plugin's own
  `insulation_level` column stays the preset's.

**"Down to the ground" by default for the terrain's classes (owner, 2026-11-11)**

On the open question which classes take `to_ground` by default, the
owner: "use the same as for the TIN; if none then mention it."

- **The set.** The classes the terrain surface is built from: those with
  the **ground role** in the class scheme in use
  (`ClassScheme::codes_with_role("ground")`, what the desktop's LiDAR
  ground and `ohl zones` build the surface from; `--ground-role` in
  `ohl line`). No list of the program's own. In the ASPRS scheme
  shipped these are the classes it gives that role, today 2, 9 and 11.
- **Three states.** `to_ground` given `true`, given `false`, or not
  given. An explicit value always wins. Not given: on when **all** the
  rule's classes are terrain classes.
- **Mixed classes are not split silently**: the rule stays off and the
  results name the classes on either side, so that the user can split
  it.
- **Said in the results**, once per rule: taken by default and from
  which classes; or, when the class scheme has no ground class, that no
  rule took it by default. The "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE" note of a vertical
  point rule without it no longer appears for a rule that takes it, and
  stays for every other.
- **This changes existing results**, in the conservative direction
  only: a vertical rule on terrain classes, in a file of any age, now
  reports a wire at or below one of its points within the band at 0 m
  — more findings, never fewer. Over points below the wires nothing
  changes (tested on a normal span; on the synthetic example with its
  LiDAR an invented 7 m rule on the ground classes gives the same
  output with the default as with `to_ground = false`).
- **Files.** A default taken in a run is never written: a file without
  the key stays without it, at version 1; version 2 is raised only by a
  given `to_ground` (true or false) or the tension rule limits.
- **Where.** The vertical clearances window (three states, with what
  "by the terrain's classes" comes to now), `ohl zones`, the Clearances
  window and `ohl line` (with it the command line's thermal clearance
  limit, which reads its rules the same way). Not yet: the desktop's
  thermal limit and the other users of rule files, which read
  `to_ground` as given (off when not given).

**Gap-type conductors: the mechanism; the source is missing (roadmap O22 item 7)**

- **What.** `bimetallic_behavior = "gap"` (wire library version **3**,
  for such a wire type only): the outer strands unloaded in each
  section's stringing state — an offset of their mechanical strain, set
  where the core alone carries the section's mean tension — and no
  compression. The knee point is the section's stringing temperature;
  above it the core alone. Ruling span and finite elements (the latter
  always through the components). With a stringing given after creep or
  load: in the initial state worked back.
- **The source is missing.** No primary description of gap-type
  conductors is in hand; the theory says so and cites nothing (the
  design's open question: build the mechanism before it arrives — the
  recommended option, taken). The model is to be checked against the
  source.
- **A choice made here: the weight.** The data sheet's weight per metre
  of the conductor **as it lies when strung** (the outer strands, most
  of the mass, unstressed at that length): conservative by the core's
  strain on its share of the mass (< 0.1 %). The design left "weight
  conservation unchanged", which on the core's unstressed length would
  have been 0.15 % light — not on the safe side. The finite elements
  keep their convention (0.08 % less than the ruling span here: 5 mm of
  sag in 6.4 m).
- **Said.** "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE: gap-type wire X (sections …) …" on
  every result of the line: valid only for a conductor installed on its
  core. On the benchmark the gap type sags **0.79 m less at 60 °C** than
  the same components as an ordinary conductor (7.06 m against 7.85 m).
- **Refused / not done.** A line's own bimetallic model cannot be "gap";
  a gap type needs a core; `ohl sagtension` refuses it (its tables are
  not of a section's stringing state); its jumpers are taken as a bird
  cage (said); the wire form's hover (the option is listed).
- **Validation.** `tbgap-001…003`, independent by quadrature; at 60 °C
  the same value from a single-material cable of the core.

**Creep at elevated temperature: the mechanism, no law (roadmap O22 item 6)**

- **What is built.** A wire type may give a law of creep at elevated
  temperature (`[cable.hot_creep]`, wire library version **3**: a power
  law in stress, time and a temperature factor, its `source` required);
  a line may give a time at high temperature (`creep_stretch.hot`: hours
  at a conductor temperature, line file version **15**). The stages are
  taken by rising temperature, each at the section's mean tension at its
  start, joined by strain hardening (the equivalent time); the sum
  lengthens the conductor in the state after creep, by ruling span and
  by finite elements.
- **What is not, and why.** **No law, no coefficient, no citation of a
  law.** The sources are not in hand: Harvey & Larson, IEEE Trans.
  PAS-89 no. 3, 1970, pp. 380–386; CIGRE WG 22.05, Electra 75, 1981,
  pp. 63–98 — to be supplied by the owner. Nothing is typed from memory;
  the theory page names what is missing; the family of forms is the
  design note's and is not confirmed against the sources (the format is
  unreleased and may change). Tests and benchmarks use invented
  coefficients, named as such.
- **The user's numbers are said to be the user's.** Every section solved
  after creep with a law carries a note with the strain added, the
  stages, and "the user's coefficients, source: …".
- **Open question of the design, the recommended option taken.** The hot
  creep is **added** to the state after creep (the upper bound), not
  combined with the creep curve by a time history.
- **Safe side.** Conservative: tension held over each stage; added, not
  merged; applied to the whole conductor. NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE and said:
  a wire type without a law on a line with a time at high temperature
  (not counted); a stage below the law's range (left out, said). Not
  covered: annealing.
- **A choice made here.** The temperature factor's `power` form takes
  both temperatures in °C (the design does not say); `temperature`
  defaults to `none`, `stress` to `mpa`.
- **Not done.** `ohl sagtension`'s `[final] hot` (its final states are
  the engine's own pair, which has no lengthening per state: a design
  choice of its own); the Creep-Stretch window's table and the wire
  form's fields (later); the JSON schema of wire files (it is version
  1's).
- **Validation.** `hotcreep-001…003`, invented coefficients: the law by
  hand; a span after two stages against an independent chain.

**Point loads with a part across or along the line (roadmap O22 item 7)**

- **What.** The object on a section's span point may carry a constant
  horizontal force: `force_across` (N, + to the right looking ahead in
  the section's order, square to the span's chord in plan) and
  `force_along` (N, + ahead), the whole bundle's, the same in every
  weather case. Finite elements only; line file version **15** only when
  not zero; OHL XML attributes of `<object>`.
- **The keys are not the design's.** The design names them `across` and
  `along`; those keys are already a box shape's sizes on the same object
  (JSON and XML). Hence `force_across` / `force_along` — the owner may
  rename them before approval (unreleased).
- **Ruling span.** It leaves point loads out; it now says so on the
  section in every weather case, naming them — the constant forces and
  (the design's recommendation, taken) the weights it always left out,
  until now said only in the user guide: "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE: point
  loads (…) left out by the ruling-span method — use FE".
- **A correction to the design.** It says the force is "not factored by
  load cases". It reaches the structures through the solved pulls, and a
  structure load case's factors act on those attachment loads as a
  whole: its part is factored with them. Said so in the theory.
- **Refused:** on a jumper's point.
- **Not done.** The object form's two fields (the form keeps the values;
  the properties panel shows them).
- **Validation.** `ptforce-001…002`: two elastic pieces by quadrature
  joined at a loaded node (500 N across: 1.848 m, a taut string 1.875 m;
  300 N along: the two sides exactly 300 N apart).

**Sag to limits: a command; tension rules by catenary constant or tension (roadmap O22 item 3)**

- **What.** `ohl tensions --sag-to-limits`: for each section in the
  blocks the largest stringing tension (at its temperature, in its
  stringing's condition) that keeps every `[[tension_rule]]`; bracketed
  from 0.1 × RTS, bisected to 1e-6, rounded down to a newton and solved
  there once more. `--write` writes the stringings back (a line file,
  or a project as one logged change per section).
- **Open question of the design, the recommended option taken.** A
  **command that writes a tension back**, not a stringing kind solved
  again on every change: editing a rule file never re-sags a line. And
  the rule extension: `catenary_constant = "1800 m"` or `tension =
  "25 kN"` in place of `factor` (rule file version **2**, written only
  when used).
- **A choice made here.** A catenary-constant rule takes w as the
  **bare** weight per metre of the wire as strung in every case of the
  rule (the same w as a stringing by catenary constant): in an iced
  case that is the stricter reading — on the safe side.
- **Safe side.** Sagging to limits gives the tightest line: least sag,
  highest structure loads. The result says so and asks for the
  clearance and structure checks after it. The tension written is
  always within the rules (the low end of the bracket), also when the
  time limit stops the search (said).
- **Coupled sections** are sagged one at a time, the others as they
  are; the command prints the check of the whole line afterwards.
- **Not done.** The window (Checks › Wire tensions… › "Sag to these
  limits…"): after the UI refactor. The Wire tensions window shows a
  rule's other limit read-only.
- **Validation.** `saglim-001…002` against an independent bisection
  (25 347 N to the newton). The design's `nlcrit` cases are not re-used
  through the line: their load states are loads per metre, which a
  weather case cannot give exactly.

**Stringing at a final condition and by catenary constant (roadmap O22 item 3; owner "go ahead and through with O22 too")**

- **What.** A section's stringing value may hold *after creep* or
  *after load* (`"condition": "creep" | "load"`), and may be a catenary
  constant (`"kind": "catenary_constant"`, C = H / w, w the bare weight
  per metre of the wire as strung). The initial stringing is worked back
  from it: Illinois secant on the section's own solve in still air at the
  stringing temperature, 6–12 solves, at most 60, never beyond the RTS.
- **Open questions of the design, the recommended options taken.** The
  value holds in the section's **own method** (FE or RS; the two differ
  by about 0.1 % of H). Max Sag is refused as a stringing condition.
- **A choice made here.** The value holds for **the wire alone, as at
  stringing**: no jumpers, no spacers, nothing hanging in the spans —
  what the initial stringing has always meant. A solve of the finished
  line at the stringing temperature therefore shows the value given
  only up to what hangs on the wire (as for an initial value).
- **Safe side.** The initial tension is higher than the value given and
  is the one the structures are loaded with; `ohl line` says both. A
  linear wire strung "after load" has no stretch: the same as initial,
  said.
- **Format.** Line file version **15**, written only when a section uses
  a final condition or a catenary constant (also in what a clipped
  section was sagged to before); OHL XML attributes `constant`,
  `condition`. Older files unchanged.
- **App.** The section form and the Sections table take the three kinds
  and the condition (needed so that an edit there does not drop them);
  the initial tension in the table's cell is still to do.
- **Validation.** `finstr-001…004`: the references of `tbcreep-001`,
  `tbcreep-002` and `nlstate-001` run backwards.

**Line parameter totals over the wires' length (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner approved roadmap O23 item 1 ("go ahead"). A span's totals were
its values per kilometre times its horizontal length: low by the sag
(0.1–0.3 %, said) and by the slope (1.5 % at 10°, 6.4 % at 20°, not
said).

- **The wire's length.** Along the wire as solved in the weather case,
  between its clamps (the sum of the solver's pieces), plus the stretch
  along the axis between a clamp and its structure at its horizontal
  length — the strain string a jumper bridges. Never less than the
  horizontal length, so no total gets smaller than before.
- **Per span and circuit** the mean of its phases' lengths (one length
  for the whole matrix, so that a span's values per kilometre are its
  matrices per unit length exactly, as before); a coupling takes the
  mean of both circuits' phases.
- **Per kilometre means per kilometre of wire.** A span's values do not
  change; a circuit's over several spans are weighted by the wires'
  lengths instead of the horizontal ones (a small change
  on a line of unequal slopes).
- **Said in the results**: a note that the totals are over the wires'
  length; both lengths in the table (Wire [km]) and
  in the CSV (a new last column `wire_length_km`; the columns before it
  unchanged).
- **Left as simplifications, said in the theory**: the matrices per unit
  length are those of the horizontal arrangement (on a slope the wires
  are closer measured square to them); a jumper counted at the
  horizontal length of the string it bridges (low by a metre or two per
  strain structure).
- **The theory** gives the formula with the sag measured square to the
  chord, the table of the slope's share and a worked example (400 m at
  10° with 12 m of sag: 1.77 % more), each computed.
- The magnetic and electric fields do not use these totals.

**A current per wire for the magnetic field; balanced input says what it leaves out (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner approved roadmap O23 item 2 ("go ahead"). One balanced current
per circuit was the only input; an unbalance leaves a net current, which
governs the field far from the line, and balanced input has none.

- **Per phase.** A circuit may be given per phase: magnitude and angle
  of each phase's current (`Settings::phase_currents`), all its phases,
  in place of its balanced current. The angle is the current's own, in
  the frame of the systems' phase angles; the window starts from the
  balanced values. Not together with the currents at its end points
  (refused): Kirchhoff's law per phase with typed phasors is a further
  step.
- **Balanced stays the default**, and says: "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE far
  from the line: the phases' currents are balanced … a balanced
  circuit's field falls off as 1/d², a net current's as 1/d, so beyond
  the distance where the two are equal the net current governs and is
  not covered". Near the line the wording of the theory stands (an
  assumption, neither conservative nor not). The theory gives the
  distance, d* = √3·I·s/I_n, with computed examples.
- **No unbalance is built in**: which net current to assume is the
  user's or an ordinance's.
- **An earth wire's current typed** (`Settings::earth_currents`): the
  same in every span of its section, carried with the induced currents
  on or off; the earth wires computed beside it take it as a given
  current. Refused together with the structures' network, which
  computes every earth wire's current — overriding one branch of a
  solved network would break Kirchhoff's law at the structures.
- **Results.** A circuit per phase is reported with its largest phase
  current and "per phase"; its phases and their sum are in the notes.
- **Format.** No file format changed: the window's inputs kept in the
  project take two optional keys (`phases`, `earth_typed`), written
  only when used; older inputs read as before. The fields plan file has
  no currents and is unchanged. Command line: `--phase-current`,
  `--earth-current`.
- **Not done.** The electric field takes no per-phase voltages; a typed
  earth wire current is one value for all its spans.

**The highest operating voltage and the insulation level of a system; the electric field's voltage (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner approved roadmap O23 item 4 ("go ahead") and added: "maybe in
the circuit table or system table where the voltage is given, it could
also be given the maximal operating voltage and maybe the insulation too
(high or low) for the cases where it's needed and by default it takes
high."

- **Where.** Both are fields of the electrical **system**, beside its
  nominal voltage (`System::highest_voltage_kv`,
  `System::insulation_level`), and columns of the Electrical systems
  table right after **kV**: **max kV** and **insulation**. (The circuits
  table gives no voltage: a circuit takes its system's.)
- **The highest operating voltage** is optional and the user's value:
  nothing fills it in, no table of such voltages is in the program. At
  least the nominal (a smaller one is refused: it would lower a field).
- **The electric field's voltage**, per circuit: a voltage given for the
  run; else the system's highest operating voltage; else the nominal,
  with the note "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE: nominal voltage used for
  <circuits>; the highest operating voltage gives a higher field". The
  result always says which voltage each circuit was computed at and
  where it comes from. The **conductor surface gradient** takes its
  voltage the same way (the same function), with the same notes — it
  had the same gap.
- **The insulation level**: `low` or `high`, high when not given;
  written only when given. **No check of the core reads it** and no
  standard's values are attached to it; it is there for design-code
  plugins.
- **Plugins.** Neither value was added to the plugin interface's records
  (`system-info`, `wire-group`): a record field changes the interface,
  which stays 0.3. A plugin sees them only in the line file JSON handed
  to an exporter. Open for the owner: an interface raise to hand them
  to the design-code hooks.
- **A plugin column of the same name** (a plugin may declare its own
  `insulation_level` column) cannot collide: it is stored as
  `<plugin>.insulation_level` among the object's `fields`, the line's
  own as the system's `insulation_level`; in the table the plugin's is a
  plugin column after the table's own.
- **Format.** Line file version 15, written only when a system has one
  of the two; OHL XML attributes `highest_voltage_kv`,
  `insulation_level`; older files read as nominal only, insulation
  high.
- **Seen on the way.** Typing `high` over the grey default `high` in the
  table changes nothing (a cell equal to what it shows is not an edit):
  an explicit `high` is reached from `low`, or in the file.

**Trees without ground nearby are listed as questionable (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner approved roadmap O25 item 1 ("go ahead"). A vegetation point
with no ground below it, or no ground point within the search distance,
has no tree base: its fall-in was not worked out and it was only
counted — not on the safe side for that point, and nowhere to be found.

- **Listed.** Every such point from which a tree of the tallest height
  checked could reach a span (its distance in plan from the span's
  swept volume at most `fall_reach`) is a *questionable* point: where
  it is, the span it is near, why it has no base. Conservative: the
  distance in plan is never more than the one the fall-in check uses,
  and a low point is listed like a tall one (its height is not known).
- **Not a finding, not cleared.** The count of fall-in trees is
  unchanged; the result carries the note "NOT CHECKED, NOT ON THE SAFE
  SIDE: n vegetation points … listed as questionable", and the panel's
  verdict is not green while there is one.
- **The counts stay.** `without_ground` and `ground_too_far` as before;
  points beyond the tallest tree's reach are only counted (no tree up
  to the largest height checked reaches a wire from there).
- **At most 10 000 listed**, the nearest to the wires (a cloud without
  usable ground would list millions); the number said is of all, and
  the note says when the list is shorter.
- **No ground surface at all**: as before one note, "no ground surface:
  no fall-in check"; nothing listed (the reason is the same for every
  point).
- **Where.** The engine (`VegetationCheck::questionable`), the panel (a
  list of its own, a click goes to the span), **Export points CSV…**,
  `ohl lidar vegetation`'s output and `--csv` (rows of the kind `questionable:
  …` in the existing columns), a saved run (results version 2 only when
  it has some).
- **Not done.** They are not drawn in the views (the list and the CSV
  give the coordinates); a guessed base (the nearest ground height) was
  not taken: it would turn an unknown into a number.

**A vertical clearance rule "down to the ground" (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner approved roadmap O24 item 1 ("go ahead"). A vertical rule
looks above and below each point within its band in plan; a wire passing
beside a tall object, below its top, was measured upwards to the top and
could pass — on the unsafe side unless the class also had a radial rule
or a screen.

- **The option.** `to_ground = true` on a `[[rule]]` with a point target
  and a vertical distance (`Rule::to_ground`, `ZoneRule::to_ground`):
  each point stands for the whole height from the ground up to it. A
  wire within the band at or below the point's height has the clearance
  0; above the point the measure is unchanged. The ground's height is
  not read: a wire is above the ground, so the column needs only its
  top. With the swing arc the same, against the band's lowest point.
- **Default off, for every class.** No existing result changes. Which
  classes it suits (buildings, masts) is the user's rule; the program
  gives it to no class. Not allowed with `screen` (which reports every
  point of its band already) or without a vertical distance.
- **Said where it is missing.** A vertical point rule without the
  option whose classes no rule of the same check measures radially or
  screens: the results carry one note per rule, "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE:
  …", naming the classes (`rules::beside_notes`; the two zone windows
  and `ohl zones`, the Clearances tab, `ohl line`). The Vertical
  clearances window cannot see the Radial window's rules, so there
  every vertical point rule without the option says it.
- **Conservative assumptions of the option**, said in the theory: the
  object as wide as the band at every height, and solid from the ground
  to the point — a point above a wire always counts (so not for
  vegetation or crossing lines).
- **Format.** Rule file version 2, written only when a rule has the
  key; files without it are written as version 1 and older files read
  as before. An older program refuses a version 2 file instead of
  checking it without the option.
- **Window.** The Vertical clearances window's rule editor shows the
  tick for a rule with LiDAR classes, its effect and its time on hover;
  the row says "down to the ground".

**Some subconductors of a bundle broken (roadmap O22 item 7; owner "Go ahead with the braces then O22")**

- **What.** `[[case.broken]] subconductors = k`: k of the n
  subconductors of a bundle break in the span. None given, or n: the
  whole phase, as before (bit for bit) — the default and the larger
  unbalance.
- **How it is solved.** The broken subconductors are taken as **gone
  from the span** (the recommended reading of the design's open
  question: of the two readings the larger unbalance on the
  structures). The span keeps one element with the share left,
  r = (n − k)/n, of the stiffness, the weight and the loads per metre,
  its length as cut; its tensions are reported per wire left (÷ r), the
  stress-strain curves take the tension per wire left, the end pulls are
  the whole bundle's.
- **Said.** On the span and in the load case's notes: "NOT ON THE SAFE
  SIDE" for the tension of the subconductors left — with the broken ones
  hanging in the spacers it is higher, not modelled, not checked.
- **A finding worth knowing.** A suspension string takes little along
  the line, so the wires left carry nearly the pull of all the wires
  behind them: one of two broken raises the wire left from 28 kN to
  41.8 kN on the benchmark (`brokenwire-004`), while the structure takes
  0.82 kN along the line instead of about 19 kN. The strength warning
  and the tension rules see the per-wire value.
- **Format.** Load case file version **5**, written only when a case
  gives `subconductors`; versions 1 to 4 read as before. 0 refused when
  the file is read, more than the bundle when the case is computed.
- **Refused** as for a whole break: the ruling-span method; a spacer or
  a jumper on a span point of the span (kept refused for a partial break
  too: untested with spacers).
- **Not done yet:** the "subconductors broken" field of the load case
  form (a span ticked there keeps the value the file gives its section's
  other breaks); the design-code plugins write none.
- **Noticed, not changed:** for a bundle the strings' weight is shared
  between the subconductors but their stiffness is not, so a string
  stretches 1/n of what it really does (0.2 mm on the benchmark); said
  in the theory, the benchmark's reference does the same.
- No schema page exists under `docs/schema/` for load case files; the
  data model and the user guide carry the change.

**A share of a span's pull per wire set at a shared attachment point (roadmap O22 item 7; owner "Go ahead with the braces then O22")**

- **What was wrong.** A structure load case's `sets` only picked the
  points; `back` / `ahead` then scaled the **point's** pull. At a point
  holding sets 1 and 2, `sets = [1], back = 0` took both sets' pull off.
- **Now.** The line keeps the spans' pulls per wire set at each point
  (`ohl_loads::AttachmentLoad::pulls_by_set`, filled where the point's
  pulls are, with the same shares; the envelope of a broken wire in
  every span keeps them with the component's break) and sends them for
  the points holding more than one set (line values with `point` and
  `set`). Line forces naming some of a point's sets take off only those
  sets' share; naming all of them, or none: the arithmetic of before,
  bit for bit.
- **Format.** Line-values file version **7**, written only when the
  values hold a set's part (`PlacedValues::needed_version`; else 6, so
  an older program still reads the file). Versions 1 to 6 are read. No
  change of `.ohlslc` (4) or `.ohls`.
- **Never a silently different force.** With line values of version 6
  such a row is "no line value … needs line values of version 7". A
  point's own value is the row without a set (`LineValues::get`).
- **Unchanged status.** A share of the pull is a load assumption: "NOT
  ON THE SAFE SIDE" stays on every row, which now names the sets scaled.
- **No new setting**; the hover of the line forces' Sets says the
  effect. No schema page exists under `docs/schema/` for this file; the
  data model and the user guide carry it.

**The bimetallic model said on the results (roadmap O22 item 1; owner "Go with O22 but not 2 4 and 5", 2026-11-10)**

- **The premise corrected.** The roadmap item first said the default
  (the outer strands in compression without limit) gave the smaller hot
  sags. The benchmark and the source say the opposite: above the knee
  point the wire in compression keeps the composite's expansion and is
  the longer one (`tbbim-003` against `tbbim-002`: 10.644 m against
  10.523 m at 150 °C, 1.1 % less tension). The default is the upper
  bound of the hot sag — on the safe side for clearances — and stays.
- **Said per line.** `ohl_line::bimetallic_notes`: per bimetallic wire
  type, its model and its sections (ten named). The default without a
  mark; a bird cage or a compression limit as "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE: …"
  (its hot sag is not the largest). Shown by `ohl line`, the wire
  tension check (`ohl tensions`, its window's notes), the clearance-zone
  check, `ohl internal`, the thermal notes, and `ohl sagtension` for its
  wire type.
- **Said per weather case.** A span whose state is past the knee point
  gets a flag (`SectionShape::flags`): under the default "NOT ON THE
  SAFE SIDE for the tension" (the recommended reading of the design's
  open question: flagged only where a span is actually past the knee),
  a bird cage "for the sag", a span at its compression limit for both.
- **No format change, no default change, no computed value changed.**
  New in the core: `Cable::bimetallic_model` (`BimetallicUse`; without
  limit = at least ten times the RTS), `Mechanics::component_loads` and
  `Mechanics::outer_state`.
- **Not done yet:** the Sections table's "bimetallic" cell and the
  hovers of the Criteria window and the wire form; the notes in the
  app's internal-clearance and LiDAR windows (their checks do not have
  the wire library; the per-case flags reach them through the warnings
  by weather case).
- **Sources.** CIGRE TB 324 p. 42–43 and p. 67 (in hand). Its references
  19 and 20 are cited as the brochure cites them: the papers themselves
  were not at hand, said in the theory page.

**Braces seated and cut against built-up members (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner, after the built-up sections were drawn as their parts: "Go
ahead with the braces". An angle bolted onto a built-up member ran uncut
to the work point, through the leg's steel, because the seat and the cut
needed a single angle at both ends.

- **The angle facing it.** A built-up section of angles gives its angles
  where its properties place them (`Shape::built_up_angles`; the joint
  details' `Profile::part_angles`). The end is seated on and cut against
  one of them (`joints::facing`): the one whose leg — the one the end
  lies on — runs from its heel out on the end's own side; not where the
  end would lie in the gap against the back of the next angle (the
  gusset's place); not where its outstanding leg would pass through the
  leg; then the nearest to its work line. A single angle is itself, as
  before, and every single-angle seat and cut is unchanged.
- **The cut.** As against a single angle, short of the facing angle's
  heel; on an inner face also short of that angle's other leg (its
  thickness). At most half the member, as before, so no member loses
  all its steel.
- **What follows from it.** The drawings (3D view, close-up, face view,
  joint sheet, member view), the bolts' places and their grip (the
  facing angle's thickness, so their length in the exports), a part's
  steel length in the part list, and Joint details' "turn it" note
  where the leg bolted is more than 5° off the face — now said for
  built-up members too. **No strength check, no finite-element input
  and no capacity or usage changes**: those read the member's design
  data and the `[[connection]]` tables, never the seat.
- **Plates left where they were.** A plate lying on a built-up leg, and
  the ends bolted onto it, stay through the work point: where a plate
  lies sets its bolts against its edges, which its checks use. Moving
