  it would change checked values, so it is not done without a decision.
- **Not done.** A built-up member that is itself the arriving end (two
  angles back to back sit astride a leg or a gusset: another mechanism,
  with its own fit of gap against thickness); an end onto two channels
  or an I or H (no heel); nesting in a built-up member. Seen on the way,
  left as it is: a single angle seated on the inner face of a single
  angle is cut at that angle's heel, not past its other leg's thickness.

**Plans and sheets: a name of one's own; name and folder last (owner, 2026-11-11)**

The owner: "for all plans, I would like the path to be given to be the
last thing to do, as well as the possibility to give the plan a name,
not just the export name given by the app."

- **Name and Folder last.** In the Profile sheets window and the four
  plan windows the Name and Folder rows stand after every other setting
  and section, just above Export.
- **Name.** Kept per plan and project line (`PlanSheet::name`,
  `SheetChoice::name`). It takes the place of the application's file
  name (`<route>`, `<route>-route-plan` …). Several routes or plans
  written at once: each one's own name after it
  (`ohl_drawing::export::named`), so no file overwrites another. A plan
  set: the name before each drawing's kind, and its one PDF named after
  it.
- **Not changed:** the title on the sheet (a field of the template's
  title block, set under *Values of the template*); the command line
  (`ohl drawing` has no `--name` yet).

## 2026-11-10

**Built-up sections drawn as their parts; the member view draws every member (owner, 2026-11-10)**

The owner, on a real lattice tower: "the double in X corners are not
well drafted as they go into another and the member view doesn't work".

- **Each part drawn.** A built-up section (two angles in a star, four
  in a cross, two angles or two channels back to back) was drawn as one
  outline with the space between its parts filled, so the two angles of
  a star ran into each other. The section library now gives each part's
  outline where its properties place it (`Shape::built_up_parts`); the
  joint details' `Profile` carries them (`parts`, `pieces()`), and the
  3D view's solids, the Detail view's close-up and its face view draw a
  prism or an outline per part, the gap open. The single outline
  (`built_up_outline`) stays for the member's size, its picking and the
  exports. Drawing only: no section property and no calculated value
  changes.
- **The member view.** It drew only an angle's leg bolted laid flat, so
  it was empty for every other member — the corner legs of a large
  tower among them. Such a member is now drawn from the side
  (`ohl_structure_link::elevation`): each part of its steel between its
  end cuts, its work line and work points, its cross-section beside it;
  its caption says that the holes, bolts and their tools are for single
  angles. A member chosen in Member details' own list is the one the
  Detail view shows.
- **Not done yet.** A brace bolted onto a built-up leg is still not
  seated on it or cut against it (the seat and the cut need a single
  angle at both ends): it runs to the work point, through the leg's
  steel. The face view draws each part as the hull of its corners, so a
  part seen end on is not yet an L.

**Field volumes: runs along the alignment, each place computed once; the run's progress in steps (owner, 2026-11-10)**

The owner saw surfaces of the electric and magnetic field volumes
computed and shown several times, depending on the spans asked, and a
progress bar always close to 100 % that then fell back.

- **Runs along the alignment.** The ticked spans were joined into runs
  in the order the line lists its spans; two spans following each other
  on the ground but listed apart became two volumes overlapping at the
  structure between them. Runs are now built along each alignment in
  its own order and stay on their alignment; the engine finds a run's
  spans wherever the line lists them (`run_spans`).
- **Each place once.** A volume takes every wire near it, so where two
  boxes overlap (alignments side by side, a branch) both computed and
  drew the same surface. A later volume now leaves the coarse cells
  lying wholly in an earlier volume's box to that volume
  (`field_views::volume_beside`, `VolumeValues::elsewhere`, a note on
  the result). The coarse lattice is still computed everywhere (1/64 of
  the points; the volume's statistics stay whole). No computed value
  changes; the surfaces of the two volumes overlap by at most one
  coarse cell at the earlier box's edge. With a tiled floor (electric
  field) the surface in an overlap is the earlier volume's, with its
  floor: said in the note and the theory.
- **Not done:** reusing a finished volume in the next run. A volume is
  one run of spans; a run extended by a span is another volume. Reuse
  needs volumes per span joined at the structures (a larger change to
  the engine), to do if still too slow.
- **Progress in steps.** The bar was the time gone over the time gone
  plus the time left, with the points to compute discovered as the run
  went (coarse lattice, then the fine points near the surfaces): always
  nearly full, then falling back. A run now counts steps
  (`Progress::plan_steps`, `next_step`, `step_now`): one per cut, one
  per other kind, two per volume (coarse, fine); the bar is the step's
  own points and starts at 0 with each step. A fine lattice's later
  rounds (a surface followed into neighbouring cells) still add points
  to their step: the bar may step back a little there.

**Where the profile's two side lines run: the corridor's edges, a distance from the axis, or under the outermost conductors of the lowest arm (owner, 2026-11-10)**

The two side terrain lines of the profile sheets ran only along the
corridor's edges. The owner asked for a setting with three choices: the
corridor's edge (as before, the default); a fixed distance from the axis,
independent of the corridor's width (the plan keeps, say, ±50 m for the
parcels while the profile's side lines are at 10 m); and exactly under
the outermost conductors of the lowest arm, following the wire along
each span. The owner's answers to the three questions asked:

- **(a) Still air.** The terrain directly below the conductor as it
  hangs without wind: no blowout, no extra distance.
- **(b) A side without a conductor on the lowest arm** takes the lowest
  conductor that exists on that side; a side with no conductor at all
  gets no line.
- **(c) Phase conductors only by default**, with a list of all circuits
  to tick in or out (earth wires and earthed circuits listed, unticked).

So, as built:

- **Names.** Template: `[corridor] profile_lines = "corridor" |
  "distance" | "lowest_arm"`, `profile_distance = "10 m"`,
  `profile_circuits = [names]`; legend words `profile_distance`,
  `profile_lowest_arm`. Command line: `--profile-lines`,
  `--profile-distance`, `--profile-circuits`. Export window, More of the
  template: "profile side lines" (as the template says / the corridor's
  edges / at a distance from the axis / under the lowest arm), the
  distance next to it, "Circuits: n of m" as a tick menu that stays
  open. The export's choice goes over the template's. A template without
  the keys is read and drawn exactly as before (a test compares the
  sheets).
- **The lowest arm, the outermost (chosen here, to be confirmed by the
  owner).** Per side of the axis (the sign of the mean offset of the
  wire's two ends) and per span along the alignment: of the counted
  wires leaving the span's first structure, those whose end there is
  within 0.5 m of the lowest one's height (the wire's own end, at its
  string's wire point), and of these the one whose two ends are on
  average farthest from the axis, a bundle counted to its outer
  subconductor. The first structure decides and the wire is followed to
  its next structure, so the line is continuous along the span; that
  per-side rule gives answer (b) by itself. 0.5 m: wide enough for the
  wire points of one arm (strings of slightly different lengths, a
  cross-arm's camber), narrow against the metres between two arms.
- **Still air (a).** The wires as solved in the case the conductors are
  drawn in when it has no wind, else the first solved case without wind
  (the app solves it when it is not yet). Without wind the plan trace
  does not depend on the temperature or the ice but through the strings'
  swing along the line, so any such case serves. Every case with wind:
  the straight chord between the attachment points, with a warning on
  the sheets.
- **At a structure** one span's trace is joined to the next by the
  straight step between the two wire ends; the profile shows the ground
  under that step. Where a side has no counted wire in a span the line
  stops.
- **The plan** draws the two lines in the pens of the profile's side
  lines when they are not on the corridor's edges; the corridor's edges
  stay.
- **Drawing only.** No result is computed from these lines; the theory
  page says they are no clearance statement (the ground under a
  blown-out conductor is not on them).
- **Not done.** The sheet preview over the Profile and Plan pages shows
  sheet frames, elevations and the lines below the lowest conductor
  only, never the side lines: nothing to follow there (the window's
  Preview sheet draws the real sheet and follows). Spans to a structure
  beside the alignment are not followed. The route and situation plans
  do not draw the lines.

**The line transmits the spans' pulls; the unbalanced load case is made on the structure. A structure may take no load case (owner, 2026-11-10)**

Another program's load-case command "% longitudinal load = p" on the back
or ahead spans of a structure was compared with that program's own
results: the horizontal pull of the chosen wire side, along its span, is
replaced by p/100 of its solved value; the vertical load from that span,
the wind across the span and the jumper loads stay. Asked where this
should live, the owner decided, in substance: **this is only in the
structure. OHL-Design calculates the forces and transmits them to the
structure; the load cases are then constructed on the structure from
those forces and applied factors.** The unit chosen by the owner:
percent (`back = 5.0`).

So:

- **The line only transmits more.** The wire solve gives, per span, the
  wire's pull on each of its two end clamps
  (`SpanShape::end_pulls`, an output: no solved result changes); the
  structure loads carry, per attachment point, the horizontal pull of its
  back spans and of its ahead spans along each span
  (`AttachmentLoad::pull_back`, `pull_ahead`); the line-values file
  (version 6) sends them as four quantities. The line's own load-case
  file (`.ohllc`) is **not** extended.
- **The structure applies the rule.** A structure load case's line
  forces take two optional percentages, `back` and `ahead` (absent: 100):
  force = sent − (1 − back/100)·pull_back − (1 − ahead/100)·pull_ahead on
  the transverse and longitudinal components, the vertical unchanged,
  then the factors (`.ohlslc` version 4, `.ohls` version 10, each written
  only when used).
- **It is a load assumption, not an equilibrium state**, and not
  conservative by itself: said "NOT ON THE SAFE SIDE" on every row made
  with it, in the solved case's notes, the report and the exports
  ([safe side](safe-side.md), [theory](../theory/structures-fe.md#a-share-of-the-spans-pull-a-load-assumption)).
  The exact treatment — the line solved with the one-sided condition —
  exists (broken and removed wires) and is named there.

Decided on the way (the brief left them open):

- *Back* and *ahead* are the span before and after the point **in its
  section's order of points** (not the line's direction); a section end
  has one side, the other sends 0, so that "not sent" can only mean older
  line values.
- Only the pull's part **along the span in plan** is sent: the wind
  across the span stays in the force, as verified.
- A clamp held from several structure points shares its pull equally
  between them; a side at 100 % needs no pull, any other share without
  the pulls gives the row "no line value" — never the unscaled force.
- 100 / 100 written out is the solved force and carries no not-safe
  note (nothing is assumed); the file is version 4 all the same.

**A structure may take no load case** (also approved 2026-11-10): until
now an empty `load_cases` meant "its type's default, else every case",
with no way to say none. Added: `no_load_cases = true` on the structure
(additive; with a list: refused as contradictory). Such a structure has
no loads in any case and no check — and is **said so** everywhere loads
and checks are listed per structure ("takes no load case": every case's
notes, the usage table as *not checked*, never as passing, the
Structures table, the line-values note for OHL-Structure). The line
results (unfactored weather cases) are still sent to OHL-Structure: they
are the forces the line transmits, not load cases. The line file is
raised to version 14 only for a line with such a structure, so that an
older program refuses it rather than computing loads for that structure;
OHL XML: `no_load_cases="true"` on `<structure>`.

**The weather case groups are read when the libraries change, not every frame; what else was worked out every frame (owner, 2026-11-10)**

A review of what the applications do on every frame found the weather
case file's modification time asked for on every frame a check window's
Setup tab is shown, to see whether its groups changed outside the
program. The owner decided, in the owner's words: **refresh on a library
change, not every frame.** The groups are read when the model reads its
libraries (a file saved in the program, Reload, another project line, an
undo of a library change) or uses another weather case file, and when the
Weather case groups window is opened — the user's own way to see them as
they are now. A file edited outside the program therefore shows at the
next of these, not at once: accepted.

The other findings of the same review were removed with it (the list,
with what each kept value is keyed by, is in
[performance](performance.md), "What else was recomputed every frame").
They change only *when* something is worked out — no value, text or
drawing — with these points decided on the way:

- **A kept value's key names everything it is made from**, and where
  that cannot be had cheaply and surely the value is not kept. So the
  project's copy of the phase-distance values is still asked of the
  project on every frame (its kind is not among those whose change counts
  the libraries' revision up), and a run reads its values file itself
  rather than taking the text shown.
- **A library page's document can only be changed through its keeper**
  (`library::edited::Edited`), which drops the text kept of it; an editor
  shown every frame says whether it changed the document (the page
  already checked the file on that answer), and the tests fail when an
  editor changes it and says it did not.
- **The profile makes notes only for the traces it writes on**; traces
  farther than 2000 px (or the view's width) beyond the view's sides get
  none. A note is centred on its trace, so one that far out neither
  showed nor took the place of one that shows.
- **Which plugins are in use is looked up on disk at most once a
  second** (and at once when they are listed again or the user allows
  one): a plugin built while the program runs is picked up within the
  second instead of on the next frame.
- **OHL-Structure reads the section library's files when their time or
  length on disk changes**, looked at once a second, instead of reading
  them all each second; a file changed in the last 3 s is read at every
  look, because a file system keeping times to the second cannot tell a
  second change from the first.
- **Lines on the ground are keyed by the solutions' serials**, not their
  points: a case solved again to the same shapes makes the lines once
  more (the same lines).

**The profile sheet: the plan between the profile and the tables, the elevations above (owner, 2026-11-10)**

The owner asked for the plan submission's profile sheet (the private LeV
plugin's template) to show the situation under the profile, above the
tables, with the pylons' silhouettes staying at the top. The sheet
templates take a third panel order, `["profile", "plan", "bands"]`: the
band rows, which follow the profile's stations, then stand under the plan
(before, always right under the profile), and the elevations drawn
"above" stand in a strip of their own above the profile instead of on the
plan. The other two orders are unchanged. A change of the drawing engine
made for a plugin's template; the owner asked for the layout itself.

**Library files merged entry by entry, a structure's labelled parts part by part (owner, 2026-11-10)**

Approved from the review's open points ("go ahead with 3 and 4"). A
library file changed on both lines was one conflict; the three TOML texts
are now merged by value — keys, tables key by key, lists of named tables
(`[[case]]`, `[[rule]]`…) entry by entry — into ours' text with theirs'
changes laid into it, comments and layout kept. Lists inside an object
whose elements carry a unique `label` (a structure's attachment points,
wire points, strings) merge part by part. What does not combine by itself
stays one conflict, as before. **A section's points stay one value**:
their order is the wire's way along the line, and a point inserted on one
line has no certain place in the other's order — a wrong guess would be a
wrong line.

**Check windows: nothing rebuilt per frame (review, 2026-11-10; the owner agreed to the change)**

A change of *when* things are computed only: the same rows, in the same
order, with the same texts and numbers.

- **Result rows are kept from frame to frame.** Every check window made
  all its result rows again on every frame, each cell written to a text
  (only Phase distance kept its rows, since 2026-11-04). A window now
  keeps its rows next to its result (`check_ui::CachedRows`) and builds
  them when their key changes: the count of answers taken, and what else
  the cells are written from (the load case shown, factored or not and the
  structure filter in Structure loads; the classes' names in the vertical
  and radial clearances; the preset shown in Buildings; the range, method,
  cases and line in Thermal rating). What only chooses among the rows
  (*Only violations*, the search, the sort, the groups) is not in the key.
  Windows: Wire tensions, String checks, Internal clearances, Lightning,
  Ice shedding, Galloping, Vegetation, Safety volumes, Vertical and radial
  clearances, Clearances, Structure loads, Thermal rating (five tables),
  Buildings (fields), Bill of materials, Phase distance and Unequal wind.
- **A table filters, sorts and groups once per view.** The shared results
  table did so over all rows on every frame (lower-casing every cell for
  the search). For kept rows the answer is kept per table and made again
  when the rows (each build has a stamp of its own), *Only violations*,
  the search, the sort or the grouping change.
- **Safety volumes:** each mesh's volume (a sum over its triangles) was
  worked out per volume on every frame for the table; now once with the
  rows.
- **The rule editors' lists** (the weather cases' names, the wire types,
  systems, circuits, voltages, what is on the route worked on) were made
  from the line on every frame by five windows, each with its own copy of
  the code. One `check_ui::LineChoices` makes them once per version of the
  line, route worked on and case names. The weather case groups are no
  longer copied per frame (shared); their file's time is still looked at
  on every frame, so that a file changed outside the program shows at
  once — keeping that by a counter instead would change when such a
  change shows, and was not done.
- Not changed: the tables of Wire fit, Line parameters and Performed
  checks (a few rows, not in the review).

Built and in active development; not approved yet.

**Merging: both kept under one id, the latest common revision, all or nothing, checked with its libraries (version-management review, 2026-11-10)**

The owner asked to improve the version management, with one rule: nothing
is copied unnecessarily (loading time) and only changes are logged.

- **An object each line made under the same id** (both added a structure
  T13) was one conflict settled by dropping one of the two; what the
  other line had put on its own (a section through it, a jumper) then
  silently pointed at the object kept. The conflict now also offers
  **both**: this line's stays, the other's comes under a free id
  (`T13 (2)`, the import's naming) and what refers to it on the other line
  follows by the rename command's rule, now one shared function. Offered
  in Bring in changes, the Merge page and `--choose KEY=both`.
- **The revision merged against** is a latest common ancestor (one no
  other common ancestor descends from), not the nearest by distance: a
  short side line brought in could make an old revision the nearest, and
  values set back since were silently overwritten. A history that crosses
  has several; the nearest of them is taken and the plan says so.
- **A merge, a revert and Bring in are one unit of work**: written to the
  file as a whole or not at all, and undone in memory if a step fails
  (before: three separate writes; a failure in between left the merge
  looking like uncommitted changes, and Bring in's two recordings could
  stay after a refusal).
- **The merged line is checked with its libraries**: a structure type's
  file deleted or changed on one line and used on the other gave a line
  that each side and the plain check accepted and that failed to resolve
  afterwards. A problem this line has already (types kept in a folder,
  not in the project) is not held against the merge.
- **No copies.** A state (the working state, a revision's, a merged one)
  shares its objects' data with the session and the other states; before,
  every status, commit and merge plan copied every object, and checking a
  state copied them again. Keeping both lays the few renamed objects over
  the other line's state. A failed unit puts back the states its commands
  replaced, which are kept as they are replaced.
- Also from the review, a slowdown of 2026-11-09 fixed: the wire-to-wire
  clearance check worked out each pair's requirement (and, with the
  altitude term, each wire's highest point) once per pair of wire pieces;
  now once per pair of wires. The results are the same.

**Merging: a rename against an edit, a deletion against a use, places, notes, bundles (version-management review, 2026-11-10)**

- **A rename on one line, an edit on the other**: the edit is taken under
  the new id (the rename told by content). Before: "deleted against
  changed", one choice leaving the old object beside the renamed one, the
  other losing the edit.
- **A deletion on one line, a use on the other** (a new alignment point
  tied to the structure, a section through it, the other line not having
  touched the structure): a conflict on the deleted object — the deletion,
  what was put on it then not taken, or the object kept. Before: no
  conflict, an invalid line, a refusal with nothing to choose.
- **The place of an object among its kind** merges as a value does; a
  line that only edited an object no longer undoes the other's reordering.
- **A note on an object the other line deleted** is not taken; the plan
  says which.
- **Bundles** are checked in full before anything is written and imported
  as one unit of work; a file cut short is refused and leaves nothing.
- `Session::ahead_behind` counts the revisions each of two lines has that
  the other lacks (for the menu's "main has K newer"; not shown yet).

Still open from the review: lists (a section's points, a structure's wire
points) and library files merged entry by entry instead of whole; the
conflicts of one logged command (a tower and its alignment point) settled
as one; the merge windows' own plans for a revert and a review into
another line taken from the session (they do not yet check the libraries
before the engine does); the ahead/behind count and a bundle import on a
joined project shown in the app.

**The Versions menu laid out by task; the line worked on always said (version-management review, 2026-11-10)**

Follows the version-management review of 2026-11-10 (owner: "improve the
version management"). No command changed what it does; this is where
each is found, what it is called and what state is visible.

- **Menu.** Versions reads, in groups: *Working on: line · N uncommitted
  changes* (a label); **Commit…** and **Changes since the last commit…**
  (the History and Changes pages of the revisions window — one commit
  field, not a second one); **Project lines…**, **New line from …**,
  **Bring in changes…**, **Submit for review…**, **Description of …**;
  **Working tree…**, **Revisions, tags and reviews…** (was *Revisions and
  branches…*, its window titled *Versions*: now titled as its entry),
  **Operation log…** (was *History…*, which the revisions window's History
  page also was called); **Offline copy ›** *Export line as bundle…* and
  *Import bundle…*; the ticks of the lines shown next to it stay last and
  keep the menu open. The *Project lines* submenu is gone.
- **Status bar.** *line: name*, with a dot while the line has uncommitted
  changes; the counts on hover; a click opens Commit.
- **The counts are cached.** `Session::status()` (a diff of the working
  state against the line's last revision) is called when the line or the
  project changed — a counter of project operations in the model
  (`project_version`), with the line's and the libraries' — never every
  frame and not while an object is dragged. *How many revisions the main
  line has that this one lacks* is not shown: the session offers no cheap
  count of it yet.
- **Offline copy.** The bundle of `ohl project bundle`, as the same JSON
  file, from the desktop app. The import asks for the line's name (the
  line worked on is never moved: another name is proposed) and reports in
  a window with a box that scrolls. Greyed out in a project joined on a
  server (there is no server operation for it; the replicas would differ).
  Both run at once, in the frame, on the project's own session; the time
  is said.
- **Words.** The app's texts say *project line* where they said *branch*
  (the revisions window's status line, its list of lines and tags, its
  hovers); the merge page and the Bring in changes window are left as
  they are for now (they are being reworked with the merge itself).
  *Make branch* is **New line at the last commit**, its hover saying how
  it differs from *New line from …* (no uncommitted changes copied). *New
  line from it…* in the revisions window asks for the name as the working
  tree does, instead of naming the line `from <id>` unasked. The revision
  list says when only the newest 500 are shown. The user guide said ◆ for
  a merge where the list draws ◎: the guide follows the list. Merging a
  review said "check it out first": it merges into its target from any
  line, and says so.
- **Deleting a line from the revisions window** says whether the line has
  uncommitted changes (they go with it), as the Project lines window
  does. Whether, not how many: the session tells the app whether another
  line has uncommitted changes (`has_uncommitted`), their count only for
  the line worked on.

Built and in active development; not approved yet.

**One window for every merge: readable conflicts, choices kept, a preview first (version-management review, 2026-11-10)**

Follows the review of the same day; the engine is the entry above, this is
what the user sees (`crates/ohl-app/src/merge_conflicts.rs`, its plans in
`merge_plan.rs`, its wording in `merge_describe.rs`).

- **One list of conflicts for every merge.** Versions › Bring in changes…,
  the Merge page, the merge of a review and the revert of a revision show
  the same thing under the same heading — "Bring changes of *main* into
  *phase 1*": the objects both sides changed, one row each, with **keep
  this line's / take *main*'s / keep both** (the last only where each side
  made an object under one id), **All: …** for every row, and a **Show**
  button that selects the object and brings the views to it. Each row opens
  to its fields in three columns — common, this line, the other.
  Before: two windows that looked and read differently (the Merge page: a
  grid *what / base / ours / theirs*), and none for a review or a revert.
- **Values in words, not stored JSON.** A position reads "moved 4.0 m
  east, 1.2 m north, 0.3 m up"; a tension, sag, temperature or angle carries
  its unit and its difference ("12.50 kN (+0.50)"); a type or cable is its
  name; a list is counted ("4 points, 2 differ"). Fields not known to the
  wording fall back to the stored value, cut short. Before: the JSON cut at
  60 characters.
- **Choices are never thrown away.** What was settled is kept until the
  merge is made or another line, tag or revision is previewed (then it is
  dropped: before, a conflict of the next line could arrive already
  settled). A refused merge — uncommitted work, a line protected meanwhile —
  keeps every choice and says why in the window; before, the Merge page
  cleared them. Uncommitted work is said **before** Preview, with **Commit
  first**. Bring in and the review/revert window ask before closing (Esc,
  the cross, Cancel) when choices were made.
- **A preview before anything is applied.** What the merge changes in the
  line, object by object, the reason when the merged line would not be
  valid, the engine's notes, and **Engineering impact** on demand (the line
  as it is against the line merged, in the weather case shown; never by
  itself). Bring in lists its conflicts and says that everything else comes
  in as it is: the session works out the full list only for merges of
  revisions (`merge_plan`), not for a bring-in (`bring_in_plan` gives the
  conflicts and the validity only: open).
- **Reviews and reverts with conflicts can be done in the app.** Both open
  the same list in a window of their own (**Merge…** of an approved review,
  **Revert…** of a revision) instead of running at once with no choices —
  which failed whenever there was a conflict. A revert therefore asks
  first: it shows what it would undo. A review is merged into its target
  whichever line the reviewer works on, as decided before; the plan for a
  target that is not the line worked on, and the plan of a revert, are put
  together in the app from the session's own merge functions (the session
  has no plan for them yet), and the session applies and checks the merge
  itself.
- **Kept as decided:** Bring in records both lines' uncommitted work first
  and is refused while a conflict is open; the Merge page takes any
  revision or tag and refuses uncommitted work; both entries stay.
- **Nothing per frame.** A plan (conflicts, their wording, the list of
  changes) is worked out when the choices, the line or the project change
  (`Model::line_version`, `project_version`, the libraries' counter) — not
  on every frame, not while an object is dragged; the Bring in window is no
  longer copied each frame with its plan. The window functions were split
  to one per part (Project lines, History).
- **Wording:** "project line", "this line's / *name*'s" throughout; no
  "branch", "ours" or "theirs" on the Merge page.

Built and in active development; not approved yet.

## 2026-11-09

**Clearance distances growing with the altitude (owner, 2026-11-09)**

The owner asked for the LeV's internal distances (Annex 6, 1: C1 at
rest, C3 in a brief approach) as a preset of the LeV plugin, and then
for the altitude increase of Table 2.4.1 (+14 % per 1000 m above
1000 m) to be a parameter of the rules rather than one value for the
whole line: "All clearance rules". `[[rule]]` and `[[internal_rule]]`
take an optional `altitude = { from, per_1000_m }`; the distances are
multiplied at the highest point of the wire checked (the higher wire of
a pair), the internal rules at the structure's highest point or the
part's — conservative, said in the theory page. The searches reach as
far as the requirement at the highest wire point of the case. The
rule summaries (the Clearances, vertical/radial and internal windows,
`ohl code rule-presets`) show the term. Not covered: the `[vegetation]`
table, galloping and the safety volumes (their own requirements; no
altitude rule known for them).

## 2026-11-08

**Line side said: thermal, jumper pull, spotting, fall-in, rigid structures (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

The thermal results say, above them, the uniform temperature in the
conductor and along each section and the steel cores' magnetic heating
(the ACSR and ACSS sections named). With the jumpers' own pull, every
load case names the jumpers whose bending stiffness is only estimated.
Spotting says its one catenary for every span and marks the terrain holes
bridged. The LiDAR fall-in says its straight trunk without a crown. The
clearance-zone, internal-clearance and LiDAR reports say that the
structures are rigid in the wire solve. This closes the audit's list.

**Line side: swing band radius, thermal limit notes, riser per stretched metre (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

In the swing band the bundle radius and allowance are taken off
vertically, r / cos β (before radially). The thermal limit says, per
section, the wire-to-wire rules it leaves out and, with a radial rule,
that a failure between two scan steps is not found. A riser's ice and
wind act per stretched metre at its largest stretch (a second solve).
LiDAR voltages above a table keep the owner's rule of 2026-10-27 (checked
with the last row, named as unsafe in the report).
([Clearances](../theory/clearances.md), [Thermal](../theory/thermal.md),
[Jumpers](../theory/jumpers.md), [safe side](safe-side.md))

**End restraint by the I/L rule and snow bridging said (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

A structure checked by its allowable loads only, in a case with ice or
snow on the structures, says that its own ice and snow are not in that
check. ASCE 10-97: an end restrained by the program's I/L rule (L/r above 120)
or worked out concentric is marked not on the safe side with what the
rule cannot know (C3.7.4: members buckling in the same case, the plane of
the stress, the bolts' centroid). Snow on members says, with every snow,
that bridging between members and snow on plates are not counted. The
load factors on components stay (owner's load cases), said in the theory.

**Clauses not covered named on the members and poles (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

Where the model's data tell that a clause of the capacity method applies
but the program does not cover it, the member or pole is marked `[not on
the safe side: …]` with the clause and never shown as passing: ASCE 10-97
3.9.3 (effective widths of compressed tubes, channels, I sections), 3.11
(stitch bolts of compressed built-up members), 3.12/3.13 (compression
with bending without amplification), 3.14 (lateral-torsional buckling of
I sections and channels), 3.15 (shear and torsion of frames); SIA 263 5.5
(battens), 5.1.4/5.1.7 (shear, torsion), 4.5.1 (a pole's buckling); the
generic pole check's shear and torsion. The moment and shear clauses only
from 1 % of the capacity (as the moments' notes); a compression
resistance given on the member covers the compression clauses. Clauses
the data cannot tell (staggered bracing, bolts in tension, a pole's
holes, connections, foundations) stay said in the theory pages.
([ASCE 10-97](../theory/asce10.md), [SIA 263](../theory/sia263.md),
[safe side](safe-side.md))

**Wind bands along the line and strings without volumes said (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

A wind band's load in a case blowing with a part along the line takes
the band's one area (the one across): its label now says so, not on the
safe side. Internal clearances name, per structure, the strings without

([Wind on structures](../theory/structure-wind.md), [Internal

**Drag factor 1, bare-area pressures and poles without P-Delta said (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

A member wind whose members take the generic drag factor 1 without

of the line's wind pressure on a member's bare area say they have no drag

**Wind: solidity within bounds, gusset plates in the wind (safe-side audit, 2026-11-08)**

Following the owner's safe-side rule: a lattice face's solidity ratio
counted members' overlaps twice (more shelter behind it) and had no
gusset plates. Now it is taken within bounds. The lower bound has the
overlaps at most once less (each member's strip clipped against those
before it). The upper bound adds the plates. The face drag and the
shielding factor take their largest value over the bounds. OHL-Structure
puts each joint's plates and splice covers in the wind on the body:
q·c·A·|n·w| at the joint, the largest drag of the members bolted onto it,
not shielded. Where the joints are not known (the line application's
checks, `ohl structures fe`, an extension's piece), every member wind
says, not on the safe side, that the plates' area is missing. Benchmark
structwind-001 moved by hand derivation (Σ Fy 2906.73 → 2910.92 N).
([Wind on structures](../theory/structure-wind.md), [safe side](safe-side.md))

**Staying on the safe side: checks not done are said, never passed (owner, 2026-11-08)**

- Owner: "what's important to me is that we stay on the safe side and that it's explained why and where it has to be done so". An audit of every treatment the theory pages call not on the safe side is on [Staying on the safe side](safe-side.md), with each item's status; batches follow.
- Owner's choices: a member end without bolts is **not checked, shown so** (no hole invented); single-angle end moments stay off by default (ASCE 10-97's curves include the eccentricity) but are **said where they would add**; the audit is worked through **structures first**.
- Batch 1a: a capacity method's notes that a part was not checked go into `[not on the safe side: …]` (`check::NOT_SAFE`), apart from `[assumed: …]`; such a member is `UsageClass::NotSafe` — violet in OHL-Structure, "notsafe" in the report, `UsageStatus::NotSafe` ("not all checked") in OHL-Design, never a pass. A welded, pinned or fixed end says its connection is not checked. Single angles as frames: their end moments said when they would add ≥ 1 %. A model without a dead-load factor says so in every run; holds to the ground above 1 N are said not on the safe side. SIA 263 bearing on the leg bolted onto: the smaller of the member's e₁ and Table 17's minimum. A polygonal pole's ice on its own perimeter.
- The example towers gave no bolts and no dead-load factor: their checks said they were not on the safe side. Owner, same day: "fill the example towers with invented data" — type-02 (and its model file) now give every member invented design data (class, connected leg's thickness, bolts with their ultimate strength, end and edge distances, pitch), the steel's ultimate strength and a dead-load factor of 1.2, all marked invented, NOT a real design; their checks are complete.
- Batch 1b, the moment along members: a frame is checked with its largest moment along it (from its end forces and its self-weight; the loads put on its joints as halves — member wind, ice, snow, surface loads — at q L² / 8, simply supported, conservative); `Loads::member` carries those loads per member from every place that halves them (the line's structure checks, the load table, an extension's own loads, `ohl structures fe --wind`); `MemberForces::{length, span_load, lumped_load}`; `check::moments_along`. A member checked axially only says what that bending would add (≥ 1 %), not on the safe side.
- Batch 1b, continued: a bowed tension-only member carries the lower of N_cr and its design compression resistance (`check::design_compression`); a face whose solidity is outside the face drag table takes the table's largest face drag (or its shape's when larger); a half of a diagonal in compression through a crossing only the other diagonal holds says its buckling length may be the whole diagonal's (`check::unbraced_crossings`).
- Plate block shear also towards the plate's side edge (one shear plane, the tension plane to the side edge), under ASCE 10-97 and SIA 263.
- Built, in active development, not approved yet.

**Bolts to the other leg, each leg onto its own plate, a joint's problems fixed (owner, 2026-11-08)**

- Owner: "go ahead with moving single bolts to the other leg also for setting up nested connections, the joint is giving a lot of errors and i would like to have a tool to help resolve errors. and also it can happen that either with a welded plate or with 2 plates that the member is bolted to both with a 90° difference so we should be able to have it bolted on the same welded on both the faces of the member or on 2 different plates if not welded".
- **To the other leg**: with Move bolt and a bolt picked, a button (key L) puts it on the angle's other leg where it was along and across; the end is then bolted by both legs (the last bolt off a leg: the other leg alone). The member view draws the other leg folded out below the heel: a bolt dragged across the heel line, or added or removed there, is on that leg (`ToolPick::Bolt`'s index: the leg bolted's bolts, then the other leg's; `Act::LegBolts`, one undo step). The code's distances are marked on the leg bolted only.
- **`other_onto`** (connection, with `leg = "both"`): the plate the other leg bolts onto. That plate lies against the other leg, is drawn round its bolts, their grip takes its thickness, and the plate checks take each plate with its bolts and the member's **whole force** (owner, same day: "stay on the safe side" — the split between an angle's legs is not known; a share by bolts would not be on the safe side for the plate whose leg draws more). Two plates welded together: a welded plate holding both faces. Data-only: format version unchanged (an optional field).
- **Problems**: the joint details record each misfit in a form a fix can be found for (`ohl_structure_link::Problem`); OHL-Structure's Joint details list them first with the fixes that worked when tried on a copy of the structure (in the background), each one undo step (`joint_fixes`). Nothing is changed by itself.

## 2026-11-05

**Radial ground clearances within the reach; `ohl zones` progress**
(owner, 2026-11-05: the radial check of a real line with a design
code's preset reached its time limit, fast at first, then slower).
Measured, not a memory problem: the memory stayed flat (6–10 GB); the
time went into the ground's swing-arc lines on spans 30–50 m above the
valley, each 0.5 m sample listing some 2000 triangles of the 12.7 M
triangle surface for a lowest far outside the reach. Now the radial
clearance to the ground is kept within the reach only (the
requirement plus `search_margin`, as `search_margin` is documented and
the points already did; a wire below the ground always counts), and a
sample's search uses the last sample's distance. The ground step of
that line: 8 min (before: past 50 min, 27 % done after 16 min); one
circuit 14 s against 619 s, the same findings within the reach — the
ground rule's lowest of 22.7 m beyond its 11.3 m reach no longer
reported ("nothing within reach"). The vertical is unchanged.
`ohl zones` writes its progress to the standard error every 30 s.
Built, in active development, not approved yet.

**Members seated in 3D, bolts on both legs, bolts in 3D** (owner,
2026-11-05: "draw them at the right place in 3d also give the
possibility to define on which surface of the member are the bolts we
might need them on both side of a corner"). Built, in active
development, not approved yet
([joint details](joint-details.md#seated-without-bolts-bolts-on-both-legs-bolts-in-3d--built-2026-11-05)).
Taken without asking (to be confirmed): an end without bolts is seated
on what it bolts onto like one with bolts; `leg = "both"` shares the
layout's bolts between the legs (the leg on what it bolts onto first)
with each leg's gauges from its own heel; `other_leg_points` for the
other leg by hand; the net section counts both legs' holes in one
cross-section (on the safe side; ends already given `leg = "both"` with
gauge lines get twice the holes they had: a lower net-section capacity);
both legs bolt onto the same `onto`.

**Lap joints, double covers and continuous members** (owner, 2026-11-05:
"have a profile slide into the other … and be directly bolted to the
other … and also have the possibility to have 2 plates on each side of
the profile … 2 shear planes", "also add the continuous … it's just one
part", "go ahead with the development of stage 1 and further"). Built,
in active development, not approved yet
([proposal](joint-details.md#lap-joints-double-covers-continuous-members-proposal-2026-11-05),
[theory](../theory/joint-laps-splices.md)). The open questions were
taken by the proposed defaults (to be confirmed): angle in angle only;
the nested inner heel ground to clear the outer root fillet; flat covers
only; the covers sharing the force by area; continuous within 1° and of
the same section, roll and reference, set by the user only (a command
proposes the pairs, nothing sets it by itself). Decided on the way:

- A continuous end is concentric but **not taken as restrained** from
  the continuity (the panel beyond can buckle with it, ASCE 10-97
  C3.7.4): on the safe side.
- At an end **with connection data** bolted onto a member, the bolts'
  bearing on that member's leg is checked too, the lower governing (ASCE
  10-97 4.4; SIA 263 (76) with the member's own e_1, not on the safe side
  where that leg ends nearer). This can lower the capacity of ends of
  existing towers with connection data; towers without are unchanged.
- The shear planes worked out from a splice's covers take precedence over
  the member's design data; planes given on the bolts still win.
- A nested end: in line and legs aligned within 5° (`NESTED_ANGLE_DEG`,
  an assumption, said); the outer angle runs on past the work point to
  hold the inner one's bolts.

**Falling trees stop at the ground; the radial check keeps its precision**
(owner, 2026-11-05: "Go ahead with trees until ground and keep precision
for the radial"). After the comparison with another program on a real
line, which lets a falling trunk rotate on through a steep slope (a few
hundred points on one steep connector span found by it only), the
physical rule stays: the trunk sweeps down to its resting angle on the
ground ([theory](../theory/lidar-analysis.md)) — marked there as not
conservative against a rule ignoring the ground. Then (owner,
2026-11-05: "for the tree falling part make a toggle in the model to
ignore the ground and continue the rotation. this is switched off by
default but can be added if decided"): `fall_through_ground` — the
vegetation window's *the trunk turns on through the ground*, a rule
file's `[vegetation]` key, `ohl … --fall-through-ground` — off by
default. The radial clearances'
swing arcs keep their 2 cm boundary spacing (`ARC_TOLERANCE`): coarser
would make the arcs' ground check faster at the cost of precision.

## 2026-11-04

- **2D only.** A charge simulation in the 2D cross-sections (per span at

  charge per bundle: exact enough away from the wires, 7 % low at a

- **The placement measured, not taken over:** the charges at
  \( r/k \), \( k = 1 + 2\sin(\pi/n) \) (the placement first suggested,
  hvlbuzz's) leave a ripple of some 0.3 % between the collocation points
  that does not fall with more charges; at 0.3 r it falls as
  \( 0.3^n \). **8 charges** by the owner's rule: the smallest count
  within 0.05 % of 64 on every benchmark (cross-sections within 0.01 %,
  closed forms 0.03 %); a setting.
- **The average maximum** per bundle (what the noise formulas take), the
  maximum and Markt–Mengele's value beside them; kV/cm rms.
- **Validated** on exact closed forms and against hvlbuzz (its
  `n_contour` 360 and 2 paths run 2026-11-04 on the three benchmark
  cross-sections; within 1e-4 by default, 3.9e-6 with 64 charges);
  `electrical-066…073` (236 cases). hvlbuzz cited with its authors as its
  `Cargo.toml` names them, FKH, its repository, documentation and
  licence (GNU GPL version 3 — the earlier "GPL-3.0-or-later" corrected:
  the project states version 3, no "or later"), with the owner's thanks,
  in the theory, the validation page and the benchmark files.

  source: the formula derived in the theory page instead, the source to

**A circuit's current in the line; the Thermal rating in four pages; one
step from a current to the clearance** (owner, 2026-11-04: "go ahead

with a setup and result and explanations of the workings (maybe also
separate the 4 things that work in 4 sub menus)"). Built, in active
development, not approved yet.

- **The operating current lives on the electrical system**
  (`System.current_a`, A rms per phase; line file **version 13**, written
  only when a system has one, older files read unchanged; OHL XML
  attribute `current_a`), not on the circuit object: every phase section
  has a system (through its conductor path) while circuit objects are
  optional and absent from older files; the voltage, the frequency and
  the phase angles the magnetic field and the line parameters use are
  already the system's; and the magnetic field's circuits are (circuit
  name, system), named by either. A system feeding branches of different
  currents is given by its end points in the Magnetic field (as before).
  Edited in Line › Electrical systems (column **A**, one command); ≥ 0,
  refused otherwise.
- **It is the default, never a second input**: the Temperature, Step
  change and Clearance pages take it unless a current is typed there; the
  Magnetic field (window and `ohl electrical magnetic`) takes it for a
  circuit given none (a note says so), a current given still overriding
  it. The window keeps only the currents typed (the 0 A it wrote for
  every circuit shown before is no longer read as typed).
- **A bundle shares the phase current equally** among its subconductors
  (assumed, said in the theory); the Ampacity page now gives the phase's
  ampacity (bundle × subconductor; the subconductor's on hover).
- **Thermal rating: four pages** at the window's top — Ampacity,
  Temperature at a current, Step change, Clearance — each with Setup
  (1 What it checks with *How it is computed* and its drawings — a new
  one for the step of current —, 2 Scope, 3 What to compute, 4 Model where
  it has settings) and Results (the shared table). Ampacity, Temperature
  and Step change compute as the setup changes (no Run; the footer says
  so and how long); the Clearance page runs on Run, with the out-of-date
  banner (the model, or its own inputs: current, ambient cases, method,
  weather case, range).
- **The clearance at a current** is the clearance-limit search's own
  solve and check at one temperature per section
  (`ohl_thermal::limit::clearance_at`, sharing its preparation): the
  steady temperature at the current in the hottest ambient case (by
  default, on the safe side) or one chosen. Per section: pass or fail,
  the least clearance against its requirement and where. Its clearances
  (failing ones, else the least margins) and the search's governing
  clearances are drawn in the views like the other checks' marks. On the
  command line a separate subcommand, **`ohl thermal clearance-check`**,
  rather than a `--current` switch on `clearance-limit`: the two answer
  different questions and take different options (no range, step or
  tolerance here); they share every other option.
- No thermal formula changed; no plugin touched.

**A weld's size and length; the plate checks** (owner, 2026-11-04: "add
weld size and length and the plate checks"). Built, in active
development, not approved yet.

- **Weld data**: `[[plate.weld]] to, size, length, kind` under a plate
  (still structure file version 9, added before the next release); the
  size is the fillet's **throat a** — chosen because SIA 263, the one
  standard here with a weld rule, defines the weld by it (6.3.2.6) —;
  no length: the seam's from the geometry, one side (on the safe side);
  `welded_to` alone still read (no size: not checked, said).
- **Plate checks** per case with the analysis, by the capacity method,
  each formula read from the standards' documents: ASCE 10-97 bearing
  (4.4), block shear by Eq. 3.10-1 applied to the plate (the standard
  states it for angles: said), net section (3.10.1), distances (4.5);
  SIA 263 bearing (76), net and block shear (82), (83), sections (38),
  (39), Table 17, fillet welds (87), (88). **ASCE 10-97 has no weld rule**
  (5.2.5 refers to AWS D1.1): welds not checked under it, none invented.
  Neither standard gives a gusset plate's buckling or effective width:
  "plate buckling not checked"; the width the bolt group's plus the
  minimum edge distances (on the safe side, no Whitmore spread). A weld
  carries the larger resultant of the member forces on either side of it
  (on the safe side); its moment about the seam is not taken (not on the
  safe side, said). Results with the FE results (`CaseResult::plates`),
  in Joint details, the 3D view's joint marks and the structure report

  accepted (the density of that local ice); with `ice = false` it is
  refused. The density is the case's `ice_density`, else the weather
  case's; with neither the case is refused with a message saying so and

  (Pa; OHL XML `wind_study_pa`; the Structures table's **wind study

able to apply ice and snow on a pylon structure"; "on each pylon you
should have a load case for structure that can be different per
structure and composed of cases from the library". Built, in active
development, not approved yet.

- `.ohllc` version 4 (versions 1 to 3 read unchanged; written at 4 only
  when a case uses one of its values): `wind_from` (the wires' side in
  the case; in a case whose weather has no wind the notes say it has no
  effect), `use_local` (the structures' local conditions for strength),
  `[[case.removed]]` (the section's wire absent: all its spans out of the
  solve, with the jumpers and spacers only on it), `[[case.broken]]`
  (several; all broken together in one solve per section; the v3 single
  table reads as one; `"every"` keeps its one-at-a-time envelope and is
  refused beside another break of its section or a second `"every"`),
  and in `[case.structure]` `direction` (left, right, ahead, back or an
  angle: 0° from the right, counted towards ahead), `ice` (true: the
  local `structure_ice`; or a thickness) with `ice_density` (default the
  weather case's; refused when computed without one — never assumed),
  `snow` with μ, C_e, C_T (defaults 0.8, 1.0, 1.0 by SIA 261 5.3.4, 5.2.4,
  5.2.5; q = μ C_e C_T s_k, (9)).
- The solver breaks several spans of a section in one solve
  (`solve_section_broken_spans`, `solve_line_broken_spans`; a point
  between two broken spans holds no wire).
- The wind bands give one area: a wind from another direction takes it
  along the direction it blows — an approximation, not on the safe side
  where the structure shows more area along the line (theory: Structure
  wind). Ice and snow go on the members with a profile (the fe check)
  and on a pole's shaft (ice), listed per structure as loads without a
  point; a type with wind bands only gives no surface: not counted, said
  (not on the safe side). Every assumption is marked in the theory page.
- Per-pylon sets: `Structure::load_cases` and the types' defaults
  `structure_loads.type_load_cases` in the line file and OHL XML; a
  structure takes its own, else its type's, else every case; names are
  checked against the library when the loads are computed.

**Use local conditions, one switch per check; weather case groups only
for picking cases** (owner, 2026-11-03: "maybe it's easier to remove the
groups entirely and just have wind for static and wind for internal
clearances, with ice on the tower, and ice and wind on the sections and
to have the button to overwrite the values"; the proposal's step 3,
approved). Built, in active development, not approved yet.

- Every check window has one switch beside Run, **Use local
  conditions**, in place of the structure and section override ticks.
  Unticked: the weather cases as written. Ticked: the check computes on
  `ohl_line::local::localized(line, purpose)`, each of its weather cases
  solved again on it (`ohl_app::local_solve`, the solves shared through
  ohl-line's memo of whole solves, keyed by the localized line, the
  library and the case). No structure giving local conditions: nothing
  changes, nothing is solved again, the notes and the hover say so.
- The wind per check: **for strength** — structure loads (and the
  usage; also the wind on the types' wind bands, times the structure's
  `wind_static`), string checks, wire tensions, ice shedding, galloping;
  **for clearances** — internal clearances, vertical and radial
  clearances and the Clearances window, distance between conductors
  (and under unequal wind), safety volumes, vegetation, lightning. The
  wire ice factor is taken by all. Not yet taken: the structure ice and
  the snow (kept with the structure; the load case library will take
  them), the member wind of the usage check and the poles' wind.
- A group's wind study column (`structure_wind`) stays as it was, taken
  by Internal clearances with the switch ticked, its runs on the line as
  written (its pressure is the case's, not times the structures'
  factors) — for the owner to decide whether it becomes a structure's
  local condition.
- The structures' and sections' `weather_groups` are read and kept, no
  longer read by the checks (a run notes them once); the Structures and
  Sections tables' **weather groups** columns are gone. The Structures
  table gains the local conditions' columns, the Sections table **local
  ice** (`Section::ice_factors_text`, `ohl_line::parse_ice_factors`).
  Line › Criteria › Calculation options gains the span rule (worst,
  mean), a field of `SolverOptions` set by the same command.
- Kept: `[check] local = true` in rule files, `"local": true` in the
  windows' setups kept in the project; the old `structure_override`,
  `section_override` and `overrides` keys are read and ignored. The
  command line does not take the switch yet; ohl-clearance's
  `CaseFilter` parameters stay (the desktop passes an empty one).
- Time: each check's last run with and without the local conditions is
  shown in the switch's hover (measured, the project's rule).

**Steel pole shafts by ASCE/SEI 48-19** (owner, 2026-11-03: "Can you look
in the code what would apply for pole structures and start implementing
it", then "What code would be needed for the polygonal or round
structures?" and the standard given). ASCE 10-97 covers latticed
structures only (1.1) and has no rule for tubes; a first try with its
effective widths for polygonal flats (3.9.3, 3.14.1) was dropped for
ASCE/SEI 48-19, the pole companion. `ohl_structures_fe::asce48`: Table
5-1's permitted compressive stress of regular polygons (up to 16 sides)
by w/t·√(F_y/E) and the bend angle, round tubes' F_a and F_b by D/t, the
combined stress of axial force, bending, shear and torsion (5.2.6), shear
(5.2.4). The pole check uses it at every height for a hollow steel pole
with its `yield` and no capacity given (a given capacity keeps the old
check); new pole fields `yield` and `bend_radius` (none: sharp corners,
on the safe side), a `[pole]` section's material giving its yield.
Conservative: sharp corners without a bend radius, the shear of the
force and of the torsion added at one point. Not yet: the net section
in tension, slip joints, base plates, anchor bolts, arms, several plies.
([theory](../theory/asce48.md))

**Bolt tools that keep the design code** (owner, 2026-11-03: "Can the
tool to add bolts or move them on joints or members actually take the
codes into account and either snap on existing lines or offer to create
a new one that respect the norm? … And if the code changes that it adapts
to the code"; asked: the force per bolt from the analysis, else the bolt's
capacity; a new line offered and confirmed; the edge taken as sheared).
`ohl_structures_fe::bolt_rules`: the minimum end distance, spacing and
edge distance of the capacity method's code (ASCE 10-97 4.5,
`asce10::bolt_minimums`; the simple check has none — a code added later
brings its own), the bolts that break them, and where a bolt asked for may
go (on a gauge line, keeping the distances; else a new line offered, up
to three; else why not). OHL-Structure: Add bolt and a new **Move bolt**
place bolts so; a new line is written only when confirmed; the bolts that
break the code are ringed red with the clause; the member view and the
bolt layout form show the minimums and the force used. Connections may
say `rolled_edge = true` (none: sheared, the larger minimum).

**ASCE 10-97: the connection and end-restraint rules brought onto the
safe side, as the standard says** (owner, 2026-11-03: "Please fix them to
be on the safe side and according with the code"):

- two bolts or more onto a **gusset plate only** no longer restrain the
  end (3.7.4.5, C3.7.4 (c));
- two bolts or more onto a **member** restrain the end only when its
  stiffness I/L is at least the sum of those it restrains at the joint
  (C3.7.4 (b); minor principal I, the restraining member's least), no
  longer when its area is larger; the ratio is said;
- **holes**: a standard hole (the bolt + 1.6 mm, 4.1) when none is given,
  and every hole taken as punched, + 1.6 mm in the net section and block
  shear (3.10.1) — was the bolt + 2 mm, given holes as they were;
- **block shear** of an angle bolted by one leg (3.10.2, Eq. 3.10-1) is
  checked, always (the standard: when the bolt pattern's centroid lies
  outside the angle's centre of gravity);
  several gauge lines with their gauges: the least of the outer line's
  block times the lines (equal shares, 4.1) and the block of all lines;
  without gauges, the outer line alone (said);
- **up to three gauge lines** in a connection (owner, 2026-11-03: "On big
  profiles up to 3 lines might be needed"; was 1 or 2): the file check,
  OHL-Structure's bolt layout (every second line staggered by half a
  pitch) and the checks;
- an **unequal angle bolted by its short leg** counts its other leg no
  larger than the connected one (3.10.2); one with no leg given is taken
  as bolted by its short leg;
- **bearing** on the lower f_u of the member and the bolt (4.4);
- the **root area** of a bolt with only its f_ub is 0.6 of the gross
  area (was 0.75), a 60° thread of pitch up to d/5.4;
- an angle's **w/t above 25** is said (3.7.1).

Results change (a real line's 73 towers, locally, against the commit
before: compression unchanged, no connections in that import; tension
lower for 31,833 of 161,937 members, median −1.0 % — the holes —, at
most −33 % where block shear governs; tower maxima unchanged for 61 of
72 towers, up to +2 % for 10, one +49 % from block shear of a member
whose two holes per section come without gauges). Tension capacities fall where the net section, block
shear or bearing governs, and members that were taken as restrained onto
a plate or a member of larger area may lose it. The structure application
shows a plate connection as not restrained; onto a member it leaves the
restraint not given (the check works it out).

**ASCE 10-97: the whole calculation on its own theory page; one constant
corrected** (owner, 2026-11-03: "make sure the theory is complete for this
code's calculation in the docs based on the asce 10 97 we can not just
have the code as reference and no explanation of the functions on side of
the program"). [Member capacities by ASCE 10-97](../theory/asce10.md)
gives every step with its clause and equation, the program's function for
it, the program's own rules (crossing diagonals, end conditions), the
assumptions said per member and what of the standard is not covered. The
code was read against the standard's text clause by clause:

- **corrected**: the upper limit of the linear local-buckling range is
  144 Ψ/√f_y = 377.3/√f_y (Eq. 3.7-2, Ψ = 2.62); the code had 378/√f_y
  (a member with w/t between the two now takes the elastic F_cr, lower
  by at most 0.1 %);
- **not on the safe side, documented, left for the owner to decide**:
  two bolts onto a gusset plate taken as restraining the end (3.7.4.5 and
  C3.7.4 (c) say a connection only on a gusset plate does not); "larger
  area" in place of C3.7.4 (b)'s stiffness I/L against the sum of the
  restrained members'; the default hole (bolt + 2 mm) below a punched
  standard hole's net-area diameter (bolt + 3.2 mm, 3.10.1 and 4.1);
  bearing on the member's f_u only (4.4: the connected part's or the
  bolt's); the bolt root area taken as 0.75 of the gross; block shear and
  the short-leg rule of unequal angles (3.10.2) and the maximum w/t of 25
  (3.7.1) not checked.

**Torsional and torsional-flexural buckling in the ASCE 10-97 check**
(owner, 2026-11-03: "is it written in the norm when a profile knicks and
turn at the same time in the failure modes?", then "Go ahead with the
code build"; the standard's text given for the local documents). ASCE
10-97 checks single angles for flexural and local buckling only (its
commentary C3.7: torsional-flexural buckling of an angle free to warp is
close to its legs' local buckling), which the core already did. Other
open shapes now get the clauses' own check, taken into L/r when larger:
I and H sections (3.9.4) and stars and crosses of angles (3.9.6) by
L/r_t, channels and two angles back to back (3.9.5) by L/r_tf (Eqs.
3.8-1, 3.8-2 with C3.8's mixed ends); closed sections flexural only
(3.9.7); a `general` profile not checked, said (3.9.8). Conservative:
K_t 1 (free to warp over the whole length), built-up shapes' warping
constant 0; both said when they govern. Where it sits (owner: "should it
be in the core though or part of a code?"): the shear centre, warping
constant and symmetry are geometry, in the section library for any code
(a later SIA 263 check takes the same); the clauses are ASCE 10-97's, in
its module. Unit tests reproduce the standard's Appendix B Examples 15
and 16. ([theory](../theory/asce10.md))

## 2026-11-02

**Field plan templates; the field-presets report one cut at a time
(owner, 2026-11-02: "Run it on [a real line] to check then add a field in
the check window with all relevant presets required and also prepare a
preset template for the export plans (where we can put a logo, choose
the point class and dxf or tin we want to see in the cut and define the
limits and colours of the lines. As well as the weather case of each
circuit and earth wire used)"; "Report per cut", "Core library kind";
"Limits for the NISV are 1microttsla and 5kv per meter"; "There are
classes for buildings only use those"; built, in active development,
not approved yet)**

- **Tried on a real line** (local, scratch copy): the building plugin
  found 121 buildings from 156 628 points of the building class alone
  (no survey codes), 187 cuts and 2 300 places. Two limits showed:
  - the ground handed to the plugin at 1 m cells (4.1 million over the

    uses the ground only in a ring around each building);
  - the report took the whole set of results at once (110 MB), more
    than a plugin gets by default.
- **The report one cut at a time** (core change, approved): the
  `field-presets` export's `report` is split into `report-cut` (one
  cut's document, `ohl-field-cut`, each call with its own time; its

  and the summaries). Changed in place: the export came after the last

- **Field plan template** (`.ohlfp`, `ohl-field-plan` 1; a project
  library kind `field-plans`, core): the title lines and logos, the
  point classes and band shown in the cut, a TIN or a background
  drawing along it, each field's limit and isolines (colour, width,

  carries the NISV limits (1 µT, 5 kV/m) as an example; the plugin's

- **The window** (Checks › Electrical › Buildings (fields)…): the

- **2026-11-03, the window finds, the field windows run** (owner: "the
  building plugin should offer a tickable list from the survey data
  classes. same for the ground codes. it should also only offer to find

- **A weather case per system in the CLI** (`--system-case SYSTEM=CASE`,
  `earth` for the wires of no system; the plan's `[weather]`), as the
