**Gusset plates seated on the corner and shaped to it (owner,
2026-11-02: "The light orange bolt seems to be of axis … Wouldn't it be
better to also have it on the plate?"; "the plate should use the corner
width it's bolted onto and try to keep hidden in the shape of the
corner"; built, in active development, not approved yet)**

- A plate lies on the leg of the joint's corner member that is parallel
  to the plane of the members onto it (from their connections; a given
  outline's plane when no member says); the members onto it are seated
  on the plate's far face (the corner leg plus the plate's thickness)
  and bolt their leg parallel to the plate.
- A plate without an outline is drawn as the convex hull, in the bolts'
  face, of the joint, each member's bolted leg from its first bolt less
  its end distance to its last plus it (1.5 bolt diameters when not
  given), and the corner leg's flange over the stretch those reach —
  no margin beyond. It replaces the 30 mm around the bolts; the IFC
  export takes the same outline. Assumed (a fabricator's plate may be
  larger); a given outline is unchanged.

**Bolt libraries kept in the project; built-up members, stage B2:
imported (owner, 2026-11-02: "maybe rework a bit the xml importer as
some of these infos might be in the exported xml … Same for the built
up sections"; built, in active development, not approved yet)**

- New project library kind **`bolts`** (`.ohlb`, the bolt libraries the
  structures' connections name): stored in the project file like the
  other libraries, copied in from `Bolts/` in the structure folder when
  a project opens without any, written to `structures/Bolts/` of the
  working copies — beside the structure types, where OHL-Structure and
  the line's structure checks read a structure's bolts
  (`BoltLibrary::beside`) — and exported there by File › Export ›
  Libraries (so an exported `structures` folder opens in OHL-Structure
  with its bolts; not a `bolts/` folder of its own). A bolt library
  imported in OHL-Structure (Edit… on a structure) into that folder goes
  into the project. `ohl line` reads them the same way; `.ohlb` may be
  added to an import (Add library files…). The plugin interface carries
  a library's kind as a string: no interface change.
- The local importer of a tower program's export (private) writes the
  export's bolts as one bolt library (each label once) and maps its
  built-up angles to `double_angle`, `star_angle` and `cross_angle`
  ([B2](built-up-members.md#b2--importing-them-s)): the root radius from
  the export's area, the gap fitted to its second moments, mapped only
  when the computed iu and iv are each within 5 % of the export's, else
  kept `general` and said. Where the export does not say whether a
  bolt's shear capacity is with the threads in the shear plane, the
  label decides (a label naming a threaded bolt: threads in; else threads
  out), said in each bolt's description — an assumption.
- First trial on a real line's export (kept locally): 13 bolts; 65 of 70
  built-up sections mapped (44 back to back, gaps 0.5–10.4 mm; 13 stars,
  0–16 mm; 8 crosses, 4–17 mm), the computed second moments within 4.2 %
  of the export's; the 5 kept general are the sections whose data are
  inconsistent (found in B1).

**Joint details of towers, stage 4.4 (eccentricities): a member end's
shift taken by the analysis as a rigid end offset (owner, 2026-11-02:
"a sideways move is needed to fit the members on the gusset plate. It
aligns the forces as much as possible but the construction feasibility
is essential … Eccentricities need to be taken into account"; built, in
active development, not approved yet)**

- A connection's `shift` moves the member's end sideways (across it,
  towards what it bolts onto; the joint's leg for a plate or nothing
  given). The analysis takes it as a **rigid end offset**: the member's
  end at the work point + the shift, tied rigidly to the joint (u_end =
  u_joint + θ × r). A frame member gets the standard rigid end offset
  transformation of its stiffness and end forces (its length and axes
  between its offset ends); a truss, cable or tension-only member's
  force runs between its offset ends and its joint takes the force and
  r × F. P-Delta and the tension-only active set work between the
  offset ends; the rigid link's own second-order terms are left out.
- **Only where a frame member meets the joint** (it has rotations).
  Where only bars meet it the moment cannot be carried: that offset is
  **left out** (the force through the work point) and said per member
  and per case — the policy of an attachment point's offset
  (2026-10-21); non-conservative for the members at the joint, marked so
  in the theory; never a singular stiffness.
- Reported: what governs ends with `[shifted: N2 e 15 mm, … kN m to the
  joint's frame members | in its end moments and the joint's frames |
  LEFT OUT …]`; the notes count the eccentric ends and name those left
  out with their moment (OHL-Structure's FE results, where the member is
  also marked *(eccentric)*; `ohl structures fe`; the line's structure
  check). No new design formula: a member checked for its axial force
  only says where its eccentricity's moment went; ASCE 10-97's curves
  for an angle bolted by one leg are unchanged (the shift is an
  additional, explicit eccentricity of the force line).
- A tower without shifts gives exactly the same results (every test and
  validation case unchanged). Validation case `structfe-015` (a truss
  shifted onto a cantilever column, by statics) and unit tests.

**Built-up members, stage B1: built-up cross-sections calculated from
their angles (owner, 2026-11-02: "plan the double star and 4 corners to
be shown or at least calculable", "Go with A"; built, in active
development, not approved yet)**

- Three shapes in the cross-section library: `double_angle` (two angles
  back to back, `back = "long"` or `"short"` for unequal legs),
  `star_angle` (two angles heel to heel in a star, unequal legs allowed:
  legs `h` along z, `b` along y) and `cross_angle` (four equal angles).
  Each is drawn from its angles (root radii included) and its area,
  second moments, principal axes (a star's at 45°), elastic and plastic
  moduli, wind width and weight follow as for the other shapes; the
  torsion constant is the sum of the angles' (joined only at the stitch
  bolts: no closed cell); each angle's own properties are kept
  (`Section::part_properties`, its minor radius of gyration for stage
  B4).
- The gap between the angles' backs is **required** (no default: the
  plan's question 1 left open); 0 when they touch.
- Drawn for now as the outer edge with the gap filled (each angle drawn:
  stage B3); IFC writes them by name with their values (no parametric
  profile), SAF as a general section with that edge.
- Validated: hand calculations by the parallel-axis theorem (unit tests,
  validation cases `sections-001…003`, calculation
  `sections.properties`); locally against a real line's tower library
  (70 built-up sections from a tower program): with the gap fitted per
  section, the second moments within 0.3 % for the crosses and mostly
  within 1–3 % for the stars and back to back (the same offset as its
  single angles against OpenOHL's: toe radii not drawn); the gaps differ
  per section (0 to about 17 mm); the torsion constants 3–6 % lower (the
  program counts the corner twice); its elastic moduli are one angle's,
  not comparable; five sections' data inconsistent (labelled back to
  back with a star's values).

**Joint details of towers, stages 4.1 and 4.2: the check takes its
conditions from the joints (owner, 2026-11-02: "Go with … B"; built, in
active development, not approved yet)**

- Each member end's eccentric and restrained: given at the end; else the
  member's flags (*one end*: the end the other end's given value leaves);
  else worked out — **only at an end with a `[[connection]]`** — from the
  leg bolted (one leg: eccentric; both: not) and the bolts (two or more
  onto a member of larger area or onto a plate: restrained; one: not);
  else assumed (eccentric, not restrained). The two ends give the
  none / one end / both ends of ASCE 10-97's curves. The rules moved
  from OHL-Structure's display into the core
  (`ohl_structures_fe::member_ends`): the Joint details table shows what
  the check takes. A tower without connection data is checked as before
  (the owner's "yes" of the same day); so an end without a connection
  now shows its eccentric and restrained as the member's or assumed
  where the display worked them out from the member's data before.
- Bolt shear, bearing and net section at each end: the end's bolts over
  the member's (a hole and shear capacity of the member's only for bolts
  of the same diameter), a library bolt's `shear_capacity` (threads in),
  `shear_capacity_shank` (threads out, `threads_in_shear = false`) and
  `ultimate`, the holes in one section from the gauge lines (staggering
  not counted, on the safe side) or the bolt points; the weaker end
  governs, named (`bolt shear at N2`). Threads out without a capacity for
  them: the threads-in value, said. The end and edge distances are not
  used yet (the standard's rules for them to be taken from its text);
  bearing stays 1.5 f_u d t on the member's leg.
- What governs says per end, for a member with connections, where each
  condition comes from (`[joints: …]`); the capacity note counts them.
- The bolt library: `Bolts/` beside a structure read by path (the line's
  structure checks too), `ohl structures fe --bolts` (default `Bolts/`
  next to the file), OHL-Structure's run with its loaded bolt library.
  A bolt in no library: said, the member's bolts taken at that end (the
  table shows the same). The self-weight factor is unchanged.
- Member-capacity plugins still receive the member's design data only
  (the plugin interface is unchanged).

**Where a member lands, the Detail view's tools (owner, 2026-11-02: "the
toolbar should also be active on the joint and member view … edit, add
and remove bolts, if necessary move the member"; "by default the forces
should all align at one point in the joint even if the member has to
stop before to fit it in place … modifiable … to allow for a practical
design"; "a sideways move is needed to fit the members on the gusset
plate … the construction feasibility is essential"; "eccentricities
need to be taken into account")**:

- Per member end `cut` (where the steel stops, from the work point;
  worked out by default so it clears the outstanding leg of the angle it
  bolts onto, in their face) and `shift` (sideways, towards what it bolts
  onto: an eccentricity, taken by the analysis — rigid end offsets, built
  as a separate step). By default the axes meet at the work point.
- A layout's end distance is measured from where the steel stops;
  bolt points stay measured from the joint.
- The Detail view's tools act in the face view and the member view (the
  close-up has none): Edit, Add bolt, Remove bolt, Member end (drag:
  along the cut, across the shift), Plate around the bolts. A bolt
  added or removed turns the end's layout into its bolt points.

**Member details (owner, 2026-11-02: "the same view of the members as
for the joints where we could define where the holes and bolts are and
that it would directly be shown on the joint side … see live the impacts
on the bar's resistance")**: a member's two ends are rows of the same
connections table (the joints' own data: nothing kept twice); its ASCE
10-97 capacities worked out on every change by the core check

run's forces (connections do not change the model's stiffness, so the
forces stay valid); its leg bolted laid flat in the pane beside the 3D
view, now the **Detail view** (the joint or member selected last).

  (`IfcMechanicalFastener`: nominal diameter, length under the head, a
  hexagonal head, a round shank and a hexagonal nut) and its gusset
  plates (`IfcPlate`: the outline extruded by the thickness), with the
  property sets `OHL_Fastener` and `OHL_Plate`; only entities of each
  schema (IFC2x3: no `PredefinedType` on fasteners and plates). A file
  without them is exported exactly as before.
- Where they go: as the Joint view draws them (`joint_details`). The
  members' solids — before, always on the analysis axes — are **seated**
  as drawn (moved along the bolts so the leg lies on the leg it bolts
  onto) when the member's bolted ends agree on the shift; when they
  differ the solid stays on the axis and its bolts move back with it (a
  note says which). Chosen as the simplest correct option: a solid moves
  only as a whole, and the bolts always go through their own member's
  leg. The placement, the axis line and the analysis model keep the
  axes. A plate without an outline lies around its bolts in their face.
- Sizes from the bolt library (`--bolts`, default `Bolts/` beside the
  file; File › Export's bolt library, default the window's), else the
  drawing proportions; no standard's sizes.
- SAF has no object for bolts or plates: not written there; CSV keeps the
  connections and plates as the file gives them.

  built; the test is ready), an import into a detailing program (O8),
  stage 5's validation and theory page.
  [Structure exports › Bolts and gusset plates](structure-exports.md#bolts-and-gusset-plates).

**The conductor jump when the ice drops (roadmap O13; owner,
2026-11-02: "Let's go with the simplified for now"; built, in active
development, not approved yet)**

- The simplified method: the jumped wire is the iced one raised by the
  rule's rebound factor × the static rise (bare less iced at rest), its
  clearance to every other wire of its span checked against the rule's
  distance. `[[ice_shedding_rule]]` in the rule file, `ohl
  ice-shedding`, Checks › Ice shedding…, the 3D layer of the jumped
  spans, runs saved in Performed checks.
- The rebound factor: no ice-shedding method with coefficients was found
  in the reference documents at hand (CIGRE TB 324 covers the static
  states only); the theory page names published studies, without their
  numbers. Owner, the same day: "keep a logical rebound factor for now,
  will be decided later … can be changed as a parameter": **2 by
  default** (the undamped rebound of a load removed at once — an upper
  bound from mechanics, conservative, not a published factor), a rule's
  `factor` overriding it; the examples and tests use the default.
- Which spans shed: one span alone by default — its iced horizontal
  tension held (a conservative assumption: the largest rise) —, or every
  span of the wire (`shedding = "all"`: the line solved in the bare case,
  the tensions re-balanced). The bare case is the rule's, else the iced
  case without its ice. The other wires keep their ice (conservative).
- A dynamic time-domain solve is left for later as a second `method`
  beside `simplified`.

  (owner: "try the new field defaults … check if cuts are needed after
  some distance"), 34 cuts against the whole line: the 2 km cut-off
  holds (0.16 % where the field is 1 µT or more, a third of the time);

  in the [theory](../theory/magnetic-field.md#cut-offs-and-grids-measured).

  reaching as far as either needs.

## 2026-10-31

**The lightning shielding check (owner, 2026-10-31: "work on this next
check"; built, in active development, not approved yet)**

- Both methods: a fixed shielding angle (outer and inner) and the
  rolling sphere of the electrogeometric model. The owner's choices: the
  striking distance typed, or from a stroke current by r = A·I^b (A, b
  editable, 10 and 0.65 by default) with a ground factor β; the
  cross-sections **square to each span** (not on the alignment: a phase
  is shielded by its own span's wires); the settings in the **rule
  file** (`[[lightning_rule]]`, presets from design-code plugins, the
  command line the same); the results with markers in the views, the
  covered zone's surface in 3D, the 2D cross-section drawing and a
  margin per phase (the angle needed, or r_max and its current).
- The sphere's test is exact: the nearest point of the free region (at
  least r from every shielding wire, β·r from the ground: for a terrain
  graph the points above an envelope h) to the phase, tried at the
  phase, the feet on the circles and on h, and their corners. r_max is
  searched at each phase's worst place per span only (at every
  cross-section it would take some 10¹¹ operations on a 25 km line);
  said in the results.
- The vendor technote that prompted it stays local
  (`local-data/documents/`, the owner: "this pdf stays local"); the
  theory cites the methods' original sources only ("please find the
  original sources and cite only the sources for the methods"). No
  first source of the fixed shielding angle could be verified: none is
  cited.
- Checked on a real line (local only): a 30° outer angle fails on its
  older 220 kV towers, whose upper phases sit about 7 m out and 7 m below
  the earth wire (≈ 45° needed): the check's figures confirmed by hand
  at one tower.

- The owner: "should be the alignment direction (cuts are made on the

  and at an angle point along the bisector — exactly as OHL-Design's
  cross-section panels place theirs. The placement was moved from the
  application into the line crate (`ohl_line::route::{Plane, plane_at,

  engine and the panels call it: one implementation, the same plane
  (the panel's tests unchanged). `CutSpec.at` is `CutAt::Station
  {alignment, station}`, or `CutAt::InSpan {from, to, fraction?}` — a
  span's place (its middle, its lowest point, a distance), converted by
  the run to the alignment station of that place between its
  structures' stations (`Line::span_station`); the result
  (`FieldCut.alignment`, `station`, `angle_point`; `from`, `to`, `at`
  now the span crossed at the axis and where) says where it went. A span
  on no alignment, an alignment not in the line or a station beyond it
  is an error saying so. Changed with it: the field windows' chips are
  converted to alignment stations (a span on no alignment: no cut, said
  under the table), Results › Open cut opens the panel at the cut's

  span-to-alignment conversion and its mismatch gone); the electric
  field's cut floor in the cut's own frame. The command line: `--cut
  ALIGNMENT@STATION[#LABEL]`; the older `FROM:TO[@F]` still taken,
  converted and said. The plugin interface (`field-presets`, built
  today, not released) changed in place: `cut { label, alignment,
  station, width, above, step }`, the host checking that the alignment
  is in the line and the station within it.

  and alignment `main` through T1–T3 (the cuts need one; its other

**The building-cuts plugin (owner, 2026-10-31: "go ahead")**

- The owner asked for "a plugin that can cluster buildings (groups of
  survey data points) and then preset the calculations of the cuts in
  the electric and magnetic field to export the 2D cuts at the exact
  points it's needed"; the plan was validated, then "go ahead". Built
  as the example WebAssembly plugin `plugins/examples/building-cuts`
  (Rust, MPL-2.0) on the core's field presets (below), no core change.
- **Buildings**: the LiDAR role `building` and survey codes from the
  parameters; a plan occupancy grid (0.5 m), cells closer than 1.5 m
  joined by union–find (the result independent of the points' order),
  clusters under 20 points or 10 m² dropped; survey points with a
  breakline id one outline each. Footprint the convex hull, or the
  cells' traced boundary (`outline = "cells"`, Douglas–Peucker).
  Ground the 10th percentile of the ground 2–5 m around, eaves the 50th
  and roof the 98th percentile of the building's points, floors
  ceil((eaves − ground) / 3 m); ids `B001…` in station order.
- **Cuts** perpendicular to the span chord as the engine computes them:
  per building the governing cut (where its box comes closest in 3D to a
  phase conductor as solved) and the cut at its point nearest the axis,
  a centroid cut optional, cuts within 2 m merged; a building across a
  structure gets cuts in both spans, said. **Places of sensitive use**:
  the corners and midpoints of the sides facing the line and the point
  nearest the axis, at 1.5 m + k · 3 m above the ground per floor, named
  `B007-F2-c1-h4.5`. Limits only from the parameters: no ordinance value
  built in.
- **Both fields in one summary**: the host runs one field per call and
  the plugin cannot read files, so each run writes its own files named by
  the quantity (`buildings-B.csv`, `buildings-E.csv`, `cut-…-B.svg`, …)
  into the same `--out`; the files without field values
  (`buildings.geojson`, `buildings.dxf`) are the same bytes from either
  run. One file with both fields would need the host to run both fields
  in one call or to hand back the files already written: not done (no
  core change).
- What `report` needs beyond the results — each building's summary and
  each cut's wire crossings — travels in the preset's notes in a fixed
  form, shown to the user and read back by the report.
- Conservative choices, said in the user guide: the top floor's place
  may lie above the eaves; a building's section takes the grid's points
  up to half a step outside it; the margin is taken from the largest of
  the section, the places' values and (B) the cycle's largest.
- Not yet: the plugin in OHL-Design (the core's field presets are
  command-line only so far); a span direction from the line's routes
  (the plugin takes the drawn direction and the report warns when the
  engine measured a cut from the other end).

**The String builder, with a torus (owner, 2026-10-31: "the builder
window with a torus")**

- Confirmed by the owner ("ok ok and ok"): a torus's `diameter` is its
  outer diameter (across the whole ring); insulator files are written as
  version 5 and line files as version 12 only when they hold a torus; the
  V-string preset puts its fittings on each leg (each leg its own string).

- A **String builder** window in OHL-Design (Line › Structures › String
  builder…; the String shapes and String library tables' **String
  builder ▾**): an insulator assembly's volumes on the strings built from
  basic shapes, each grounded, electrified or insulated — presets (I
  string, V string's legs, double string), the common fittings in one
  click (top fitting, insulator, arcing horns, clamp, grading ring,
  yoke), each field explained beside it, a front and side preview in the
  string's own axes in the states' colours. Saving writes the assembly's
  file through the String shapes table's path (one undoable change). The
  presets' sizes are invented starting values, said so.
- A new shape kind, the **torus** (a grading ring): around the string's
  axis, square to it; `diameter` its **outer** diameter (what a rule
  across the ring measures), `tube` its tube's diameter (below half the
  outer one). A format change: an `.ohli` with a torus is written as
  **version 5** (a program reading version 4 refuses it by its version,
  not by an unknown kind; without a torus the file stays 4 or older), a
  line file with one among a string's own shapes as **version 12** (else
  11 or older); the OHL XML's `<shape>` takes `tube`.
- The internal clearances measure a torus — the one volume that is not
  convex — **exactly against points and spheres** (closed form), and
  against segments, triangles, boxes, cylinders, cones and other tori **by
  the chords of its circle**, each grown by the tube and the chords'
  sagitta: never farther than the exact distance (**conservative**), at
  most 0.5 mm nearer (1 mm between two tori), the chords' count chosen
  from the ring's size (sagitta ≤ 0.25 mm). Marked as conservative in the
  theory page.

**The electric field's charges where the wires are; its floors side by
side (owner, 2026-10-31)**

- The owner asked for the 2D field on a cut of a circuit next to hvlbuzz's:
  on the example double circuit (T1–T2, mid-span) the program read 3.6 %
  low at the axis — its charges came from the span's mean cross-section
  (the wires at their mean height), the field from where the wires hang
  at the profile: not conservative. Given the same cross-section, both
  agree within 0.2 %. The owner: "go ahead but keep in mind some
  differences can happen due to the 2D/3D methods". The charges now from
  the cross-section where they are: in 2D the profile's or point's own;
  in 3D each span in 16 stretches, each at the charges of the
  cross-section at its middle (`electric::STRETCHES`). 2D now equals
  hvlbuzz on that cross-section (a crate test, hvlbuzz's project and
  profile in `benchmarks/electrical/hvlbuzz/D-example-double-circuit-T1-T2*`);
  3D 0.6–0.8 % above it at the largest value. On a real line the profiles'
  largest values moved by −3.3 % to +4.9 % (one low span +15.6 %).
- The owner: "try the computations of the 3D over a span and see for
  time optimisations". Measured on one 300 m span: the profile's floor
  (4 660 tiles) 7.5 s, nearly all of it its dense LU on one core; a
  volume's floor 1 s, its points 0.6 s (2 m) to 2.3 s (1 m). Now the
  profiles' floors solved up to 4 at once (as many as about 1 GB holds),
  the line's potential at the tiles on all cores, the stretches' charges
  on all cores, a slow power replaced by the exact \( r^2\sqrt{r^2} \):
  4 real spans' profiles 15 s instead of 52 s, the values unchanged by
  these. The progress counts floors solved side by side.
- The owner, asked how much a parallel LU would bring (measured on
  floor-like systems: 14× at 2 850 tiles, 22× at 4 660, 31× at 8 000, the
  same solutions to 1e-14): "go ahead with faer" (the tech stack's choice
  for large dense systems, ADR 0002). The floors' LU now faer's on all
  cores, filled column by column into one table; 4 real spans' profiles
  4.5 s (52 s in the morning); two floors side by side. "Make sure we can
  keep memory not too high … laptops with 16 up to 32 GB": a floor's
  memory counted (16 bytes per pair of tiles: its table and its factors),
  side by side as many as 1 GB holds, one over 2 GB refused, said; the
  window says a volume's longest run's floor (tiles, memory, time) before
  Run, in red over the limit. `TiledFloor::seconds` measured again (0.8 s
  for the table and the potentials at 4 660 tiles, growing with the
  square; 0.4 s for the LU, with the cube).
- The owner asked whether the electric field takes the structures'
  steel into account near the pylons (it did not), then "plan it" and
  "off by default, if only 1 leave off, yes": the structures' steel
  earthed, an option off by default — each structure's members (detail
  levels 2 and 3, else its own stick drawing; level 1 left out, said) in
  pieces of at most 3 m solved with each tiled floor they stand on (the
  floor's unknowns the tiles and the pieces; the line's charges as
  without the steel); not with the plane under each point nor in 2D
  (said); tested against the exact 2D result of an earthed bar (0.4 %);
  the window's 3 Model and `--steel`. And profiles **beside the
  structures** (both field windows): a given distance (10 m) into each
  ticked span from both its structures.
- The owner looked at a valley span of a real line (2D cut with isolines,
  3D volume at 5 kV/m) and asked to fix three things, then "the same for
  the magnetic field": (1) the cross-section panel opens **on the wires**
  while a field is drawn in it (the conductors crossing the cut, 15 m
  around them; re-fitted when the field arrives, the camera untouched;
  **Whole cut** / **Zoom to the wires**); (2) **thin, short pieces of a
  volume's surfaces left out** (at most 2 steps across in two directions,
  20 long: beads along an earth wire), counted with the results — display
  only; (3) the command line's **ground by default the project's** (its
  surface of the checks, else its point cloud's ground along the whole
  line, as OHL-Design), straight between the feet only for a line file,
  said as a warning: across the valley the straight ground passed close
  under the wires (14.5 kV/m at 1 m instead of 0.007) and dropped six
  sections' charges as "at or below the ground". Both fields (the panel
  and the volumes are shared; the magnetic command's points too).
- Explained to the owner (asked "what is the fundamental role played by
  these tiles"): the ground's induced charge, solved so the ground stays
  at zero potential; each tile's charge acts on every other's, hence a
  table of tiles². A plain cut-off by distance is not taken (a tile's
  effect falls only as 1/distance while the tiles at a distance grow with
  it); coarser far tiles, a floor per span and compressed far groups
  (fast multipole, H-matrices) are the sound ways. Open: volumes' floors
  per span (asked), a measured smaller reach.

**The magnetic field: continuous tiles, the jumpers and the structures'
currents (owner, 2026-10-29)**

- The owner: "yes" to joining the views' tiles, "and also include
  jumpers and pylons steel to improve accuracy".
- Tiles: grids from above and volumes laid on one path along each run of
  spans following each other (`field_views::Path`): mitred offsets at the
  line angles, the direction turning evenly along each straight, the
  lattice ending exactly at the run's ends — no gap or overlap at the
  structures. The volume's cells near a wire found by distance (any
  path). A level met exactly at a lattice point shares that point's
  vertex (no crack).
- Jumpers: on by default; between two section ends of one phase, the
  phase's current from the end it comes in by to the end it leaves by;
  taps, mixed phases left out and said.
- Found on the way (a fault since 2026-10-27): each span took the
  current's direction from its own structures' order, so where that order
  turned a current left a structure by both sections (on a real line all
  526 jumpers were refused for it, 3 of 77 profiles moved by more than
  1 %, one by 9.7 %), and off the alignments a section drawn backwards
  made a span of its own. Now a circuit's current follows its chain of
  sections and jumpers, each chain turned to run along the line over most
  of its length; off the alignments a span takes the way most sections
  are drawn (`cross_section::line_spans`). With the jumpers, profiles at
  a steep span's lowest point near a structure (7–8 m away) rose up to
  2.8 times on that line: the 14 m jumpers carry 1000 A close by.
- The structures' steel: its currents modelled — the earth wires as a
  network over the line through every structure's **earthing
  resistance** (new: `Structure.earthing_resistance_ohm`,
  `ElectricalSettings.earthing_resistance_ohm`; 10 Ω assumed when not
  given, said; Structures table **earthing Ω**, the structure's window,
  Line parameters), the structures' currents as paths down their axes.
  Its magnetic permeability is not modelled: a 5 cm member disturbs the
  field by under 0.25 % at 1 m (the theory's estimate); a finite-element
  model of a tower would be needed. On the synthetic double circuit the
  network gives 2.3 A in the earth wire where the infinitely long earth
  wire gave 94 A.
- The electric field's ground, asked "what's easier and actually
  better" (answered, to confirm by the owner): a plane fitted under each
  point (images in it), continuous
  along the line, easier, and enough where ordinances ask (1 m above the
  ground; objects matter more than the terrain's curvature); a
  conducting terrain surface later if measured to matter.

  for the 3d but make sure to check the performance"; levels as rules on
  what is displayed; "change most of the line modelisation parameters …
  but it should always explain the difference it makes on the results and
  the calculation time". The electric field comes after this.
- Built: the levels as a table (value, colour, shown; display only, the
  limit addable); isolines from above (the grids, their own step); the
  field in **every cross-section panel open** (computed from the run's
  wires when a panel opens or moves); **volumes** over spans
  (isosurfaces, translucent in the 3D view; `--obj`). Generic for any
  field (`ohl_electrical::field_views`, `contour`), so the electric field
  takes the same views.
- Settings with their effect and time beside them: the wire pieces (as
  solved, or at most a length — new points on the curve through the
  solver's points), the wires modelled (the whole line by default, or
  within a distance of each cut and volume), each view's step. Every run
  **measures** how far its isolines and surfaces lie off their levels and
  what the wires left out change (the field computed again at up to 200
  of their points), instead of assuming it.
- Performance, checked on a real line (28 km, 7 circuits, 124 000
  pieces): the sum arranged per polyline (half the square roots; equal
  within rounding) and per block of 64 points (the wires stay in the
  cache), threads taking blocks in turn; a volume's fine lattice only
  where a surface passes (about half of it). One span at 2 m: 85 s → 67 s
  with the whole line, 6 s with the wires within 2 km (the field within
  0.03 %); 1 m about four times longer. The computer slows to about half
  speed after 5 s of full load: the estimates use the last run's speed.
  The whole line stays the default (quality before speed).
- To do, as options (owner): the **jumpers** as current paths and the
  **structures' steel** (roadmap O18 step 4).

**A span stays on the profile with another line under it (owner, 2026-10-29)**

- Reported: the line's wires were missing on the sheets and in the
  profile view where a crossing line passes under a span. A structure of
  the crossing line standing within 5 m of the alignment is in the run
  of the line (`NEAR_ALIGNMENT`), so the two structures of the span no
  longer followed each other in the run and the span was left out.
- A structure near the alignment that is not tied to one of its points,
  with a span of the line along the alignment passing over it and none
  of its own spans along it, is not of the line's run: it is away
  (`Line::alignment_views`), so the spans ahead, line angles, the sheets'
  bands and height steps are those of the line itself (TR-type example:
  706.6 m instead of 69.4 + 637.2 m). A span between two structures of
  the run is also drawn when it stays within 5 m of the alignment over
  its whole length (`AlignmentView::along`; the profile, the sheets and
  the profile's lines on the ground use it).
- The owner's rule for what is drawn: the line itself always; besides
  it, every structure of the line within the line width (beside the
  route, not on it: `Mark::beside`) and every span or jumper passing
  within it (a crossing, an outgoing or ongoing connection), cut at the
  line width. They never take the line's own spans away, and a structure
  beside is on no span of the bands' sags.
- `tools/check.sh` (owner, 2026-10-29): the full local check before a
  push, kept in the repository instead of a session folder; its private
  parts (the real-line scan's names, private plugins) are read from
  `local-data/check/` only where it exists. It checks the documentation
  links too (three links to a renamed heading fixed).

**Structure solver guards: implausible displacements, stalled P-Delta (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- From a comparison of the structure analysis with a commercial tower
  program on a real line's lattice towers (kept privately): a
  near-mechanism (a joint whose four members lie 0.1° off one plane,
  above the stabilisation threshold of about 0.06°) solved "successfully"
  with displacements of 200 km and usages of 50 000 %, and P-Delta on
  another tower stalled at 6.4·10⁻⁸ after 200 iterations (tolerance
  10⁻⁹).
- **Implausible displacements are an error**: a joint moving more than
  half the structure's size (`IMPLAUSIBLE_SHARE`) is not returned; with
  stabilisation on, the solve is repeated with the translations held at a
  looser threshold (1.2·10⁻⁵ of the joint's largest stiffness, about 0.2°,
  justified by coordinates rounded to four significant digits: 5 mm at
  10–99 m over a 1.5 m member) and refused ("implausible displacements …",
  naming the joints) when they still move that far. A buckling failure is
  retried the same way. A model that solves plausibly is unchanged bit for
  bit; the looser threshold, when used, is said in the notes.
- **A P-Delta solve stopped just above the tolerance is accepted** when
  the out-of-balance forces are below 10⁻⁶ of the loads, flagged
  (`Solution::stalled`) and said in the notes with the residual reached;
  chosen over the full tangent (quadratic convergence) as the smaller
  change. Above 10⁻⁶ it stays refused. Theory page: Second order, Joint
  stabilisation.
- To confirm: the limit of half the structure's size (an error, no
  warning level below it), and 1.2·10⁻⁵ for the second try.

**Electric and magnetic fields in the core, magnetic field first (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- The owner asked for the electric and magnetic fields, the magnetic
  field first. Biot–Savart and the line charges are textbook, so the
  fields join the line parameters in `ohl-electrical`; an ordinance's
  limits and rules (for Switzerland the NISV: 1 µT at places of sensitive
  use, the thermal limit current, the governing load-flow directions)
  come from a plugin's parameter file. The hvlbuzz plugin stays for the
  audible noise and as a cross-check of the fields. Draft in ROADMAP O18
  steps 4 (magnetic field) and 5 (electric field); reference the BAFU's
  NISV enforcement guide (2007 draft, sections 2.4, 8.1.4, 8.7).

**Magnetic field, first slice: the choices made (roadmap O18 step 4, 2026-10-27; to confirm by the owner)**

- **What is reported**: B, the rms of the vector (the guide's equation 2,
  IEC 62110's resultant field), and beside it the cycle's largest value
  (the ellipse's semi-major axis, as an rms value). Two frequencies: each
  apart, added as the root of the sum of squares (the guide's equation
  3); the largest value likewise (only an indication).
- **3D** on the solver's polylines, each subconductor its own polyline
  (the views' bundle geometry), the current shared equally; closed-form
  Biot–Savart per straight piece; the whole line modelled. Jumpers and
  the ground's return currents left out (said; the latter estimated at
  hundredths of a µT in the theory page). Steel not modelled.
- **2D** takes the wires **where they cross the profile** by default (at
  the lowest point: conservative against 3D), not the span's mean height
  the roadmap draft named (not conservative under the lowest point); the
  mean is an option. Warnings: a line angle over 5° at a structure within
  the profile's half width (or the limit line's reach) of the station; a
  span whose wires' places relative to each other differ by more than
  **0.5 m** between its ends (the tolerance is the program's choice).
  Crossings are not checked (no other lines yet).
- **Stations**: every span's lowest point = the lowest point of its
  lowest phase conductor (height above the ground), projected on the
  span's axis; profiles square to the span's axis.
- **Currents**: per circuit (a system's phases in one named circuit),
  matched by its name, its system's id or `*`; a circuit without one
  carries 0 A (said). Direction: *along the line* = from its first
  structure to its last; *reverse* turns every phase by 180°. The thermal
  rating (command line `--thermal`): the least over the circuit's sections
  of bundle × ampacity (`ohl-thermal`, now a dependency of
  `ohl-electrical`), the ambient case and the conductor temperature typed
  — no ordinance's conditions built in. Not in the window yet.
- **Earth wire currents**: \\( -Z_{ee}^{-1}Z_{ep}I_p \\) per span from its
  mean cross-section and the line parameters' primitive matrices (the
  line's earth return method and soil resistivity). On the synthetic
  example they **raise** the field near the ground by about 5 % (the
  induced current nearly in phase with the lowest phase) — the roadmap
  draft expected a slight reduction; it depends on the arrangement.
- **Modelled length**: the reach is measured on the profile (the farthest
  point at or above the limit from the nearest conductor at the station;
  without a limit the profile's half width); a station closer to the
  line's end than five times it is warned about.
- **Points**: a CSV with `x`, `y`, `z` or `height`, optional `name`; each
  placed beside the nearest span (for its ground and, in 2D, its
  cross-section).
- The window holds its inputs for the session only (not saved with the
  project yet); the computation runs on all cores (scoped threads), with
  progress and Stop.
- `ohl electrical parameters` and `magnetic` take their arguments boxed
  (clippy's size rule); no behaviour change. `cross_section` exposes its
  span axis and phase data to the crate (no behaviour change).

**Soil resistivity measured at the structures (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- Every structure may carry the soil resistivity measured at it, Ω·m
  (`Structure.soil_resistivity_ohm_m`; none: not measured), typed in the
  Structures table's **soil ρ Ω·m** column or the structure's window.
  First taken as the footing (earthing) resistance in Ω; the owner
  corrected it to the soil resistivity.
- The line parameters take on each span the **geometric mean** of its two
  structures' values (one measured: that one; neither: the line's
  `electrical` value, else 100 Ω·m assumed and said with the number of
  spans). Geometric because the earth return's depth goes with √ρ and the
  impedance with its logarithm; an arithmetic mean would weigh the higher
  value more.
- Line file version 11 when one is given (older programs refuse the
  field); OHL XML attribute `soil_resistivity_ohm_m` on `<structure>`;
  projects keep it with the structure. `ohl electrical parameters --soil`
  sets the line's value; measured structures still give theirs.

**Electrical module, first part: cross-sections and line parameters (owner, 2026-10-27; roadmap O18 steps 0 and 1)**

- A headless crate `ohl-electrical` (no GUI, no plugin calls). The
  **cross-section** (`CrossSection`) is the one record the electrical
  calculations share: per span of the line, at a station or as the span's
  mean, every conductor and earth wire with its offset (to the right
  looking ahead), height above the ground under it, bundle, wire data
  (diameter, GMR, AC resistance at the case's temperature) and system,
  phase, circuit, voltage, frequency, angle; the ground (elevation, slope
  across, soil resistivity). Other lines' wires: an empty extension point.
  Serialisable, for the plugins later; the plugin interface is unchanged.
- **Line parameters**: series impedance with earth return by **Carson's
  series** (default; the asymptotic expansion above a = 15), or the
  **complex depth** (Deri et al. 1981), or **Carson's first terms**
  (modified Carson, for comparison); earth wires reduced out by Kron
  (**continuously earthed**, an assumption); capacitance from potential
  coefficients with images (perfect earth, ε₀); bundles as one
  equivalent wire. Per span, summed per circuit (phases of one system with
  one circuit name) by phase, so a transposition along the line is in the
  totals; stretches of the same sections; sequence values of the ideally
  transposed line and the coupling of the sequences as built; zero
  sequence coupling between circuits on the same spans.
- **Height in a span**: the solved wire's exact average (default) or the
  textbook attachment height minus 2/3 of the sag — a line setting.
- **Soil resistivity**: a new line setting (with the earth return method
  and the height rule: `Line.electrical`, line file **version 11** when
  not the defaults, project meta row `electrical`, OHL XML
  `<electrical>`). Not given: **100 Ω·m assumed**, the value the IEEE
  distribution test feeders assume (IEEE PES DSAS, "Radial Distribution
  Test Feeders", 2000), said in every result and in the window — never a
  hidden constant. One value per line; along the route later.
- **Capacitance over a transposition**: the program averages the
  capacitances (stretches in parallel at one voltage); textbooks average
  the potential coefficients (equal charges) — 0.7–1.4 % apart on the
  lines checked. The program's choice is the physical one; the validation
  case checks the textbook value from the program's matrices. *To confirm
  by the owner.*
- Frequency from the system, 50 Hz when it gives none (said); DC systems
  left out of the AC parameters (said).
- `ohl electrical parameters` and Checks › Electrical › Line parameters…
  (the Analysis items of OHL-Design are in its Checks menu). Validated
  against Kersting's Example 4.1 as printed in Overbye's open ECEN 667
  lecture (2019), Overbye's triple-bundle example, and Carson's integral
  by quadrature (13 cases); see [Line parameters](../theory/line-parameters.md).

**The server encodes each broadcast once (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- Left open on 2026-10-26 (see "Not done" there): every broadcast
  (edits, locks, the users' list) was serialised to JSON once per client,
  in each client's writer, and the message itself copied per client by
  the broadcast channel. Now `server::Event::new` encodes it once
  (`Utf8Bytes`, a shared buffer) and shares the message (`Arc`): the QUIC
  writer writes those bytes (`write_encoded`, the same length prefix and
  64 MiB limit), the web client's writer sends them as its text frame.
  Answers and notices of one client are still encoded by its writer.
- Behaviour identical: the same JSON, the same order (the answer right
  after its edit), the same limits; tests that every receiver holds one
  buffer and that three users receive the same edit.

**Library files the export lacks are added on project import (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- An export cut off before its cable data imported with no cables and
  every section unsolved. File › New project from another program… and
  Import › Another project into this one… now have **Add library
  files…** (files picked; their kind from the extension,
  `ohl_io::projects::LIBRARY_EXTENSIONS`: the project's library kinds
  but the structure loads); the command line `--library FILE`
  (repeatable) on `ohl project import-from` and `import-into`.
- They are added to what the plugin read before anything else
  (`ImportedProject::add_libraries`): before *clip in*, which needs the
  wire types; a file of the same kind and name as one read replaces it;
  each is noted. Into an existing project they are therefore merged by
  the rules of the import's own files (cables by id into the project's
  wire file). A file of no library kind is refused before reading.
- No format changes.

**Replace mode: sections crossing the stretch's end are split; circuits the variant lacks are removed (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- A project section running through a tower the variant removes and on
  beyond the stretch's end was removed whole, the part outside too. Now
  it is split at the end: its spans with an end outside the stretch stay
  as a section of their own (the first piece under its id; span points,
  local winds and stringing of those spans kept — a clipped-in section's
  lengths, a sag in a span left out taken in the ruling span;
  `Section::piece`), the part inside goes.
- Inside the stretch, the sections of a circuit the variant does not carry
  at all (e.g. one the variant re-equips a tower without) stay removed by
  default, as for the others; the list offers to keep them.

**Imports get everything in, the rules are checked afterwards; curves held flat (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- The owner: "what's important is that the imports get everything in; the
  rules are to be checked afterwards." A wire file is no longer refused
  for one faulty wire type: the wire library leaves that wire type out
  with its reason (`Library::skipped`) and loads the rest; the import
  keeps the file as the export gave it (safe mode no longer strips
  cables), and the reasons are shown when the library loads (app load
  log and library page, `ohl line` warnings).
- A stress-strain curve that stops rising before 1 % strain, without a
  range given (as some programs export it; an OPGW's aluminium layer turning
  at 0.63 %), was refused. The owner chose to accept it and hold the
  curve flat from where it stops rising: the layer takes no more load
  beyond, the wire stretches more (conservative for clearances, marked as
  such in the theory page), said when the library loads and warned about
  in every state beyond it. With a range given, a curve that turns inside
  it is still left out (the data contradict themselves).
- Another project into this one: a merged line that does not check (a
  variant labelling the phases or systems of a conductor the project
  continues otherwise — a by-pass reconnecting circuits) was refused at
  Import. It is now mended as safe mode mends a plugin's line (the later
  section of a joined pair takes the first's system and phase, same
  voltage; else the joining jumper is left out), each mend said in the
  notes, to be checked afterwards. **In Replace mode the variant's names
  win** (owner, 2026-10-27: the variant is the new state): a project
  section joined to an imported one takes the imported one's system and
  phase, and the names run along the whole conductor (the project's
  sections outside the stretch too); in Add mode the project's win.
- Versions › Project lines › Working tree (owner report, 2026-10-27): the
  lanes were in the order of the lines' names, and the revisions claimed
  in that order, so a variant whose name sorted first was drawn above the
  line it came from and could take that line's revisions. The lines now
  claim their revisions in the order they were made (the main line first;
  a line after the one it started from), and each is drawn just below the
  line it started from (its "from" note, else where its history meets
  another's).
- Versions › Project lines › Working tree: a project line with nothing
  of its own committed and uncommitted work was drawn joined to its
  source twice (its start ring and its open dot); the open dot now follows
  its start ring (owner report).

**Another project into this one: Replace mode for a variant, a window that fits (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- **The window was too big**: with many objects in both, Import went off
  the screen and the window did not scroll. Now what is to settle
  scrolls (its height kept to the screen), and the summary line, Import
  and the status stay below it.
- **Replace mode, the default** (`ohl_io::import_into::ImportMode`;
  `ohl project import-into --mode replace|add`): "usually each thing that
  is the same in both should be replaced by the new one", and an import
  that covers part of the line is a variant of that stretch — the line
  outside it kept, inside it the import's towers, sections and jumpers
  instead of the project's. What appears in both defaults to the
  imported one (cables too: the imported cable replaces the project's in
  its wire file, under its id; *keep both* stays a choice, never the
  default). A tower in both is the imported tower (choice per tower,
  key `tower:<id>`); the project's sets it lacks stay on it where what
  the line keeps hangs on them. A tower of another id at the same place
  takes the imported id, what refers to it following.
- **The stretch**: two towers in both the import goes between with no
  other tower in both between them (along its sections, over its own new
  towers too; along its alignments when it has no section) mark a gap;
  the project's structures in that gap along its alignments or sections
  are removed, with the sections at them and those over towers in both
  only whose spans the import covers, and the jumpers at them or with
  every end inside the stretch. Jumpers and sections at the stretch's end
  towers that go on outside are kept. A section that runs out of the
  stretch through a removed structure goes with it (a note says so).
  Every removal is listed with why and a choice to keep it (key
  `remove:structure|section|jumper:<id>`). An imported alignment on one
  of the project's replaces the part between their first and last points
  in common.
- **Add mode** is the behaviour before: the project's kept, nothing
  removed.
- Checked on a real export pair (a variant of a stretch of a line, kept
  out of the repository): the stretch's three structures not in the
  variant and their sections and jumpers removed, the tower at the same
  place under the variant's id, the new tower added, the line checks;
  the sections that do not solve are only those on two cables whose ids
  the wire library refuses (spaces in the id, from the export).

**Safe mode for projects from other programs; solid wires filling their circle (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- Exports with faults (an id given twice, empty values, joined sections
  given two systems, a wire file with a cable twice or one that does not
  load) refused the whole import. The owner asked for a safe mode that
  imports what is there with a warning that some things may be missing.
  The host now reads a project plugin's line and wire files as far as they
  read (`ohl_io::projects::line_safe`, `safe_cables`), each fault said as a
  `warning:` in the notes; nothing is refused for one fault. Two joined
  sections of different systems of the same voltage take the first's
  system and phase rather than losing the jumpers between them (an export
  naming one conductor two ways); of different voltages, the jumper is
  left out.
- A cable's area was refused when it exceeded its diameter circle by any
  amount; a solid 50 mm² wire of 8.00 mm (50.3 mm² both, rounded) failed.
  The check guards against unit mistakes (factors of 10 or more): it now
  allows 1 % over the circle for rounded data.

**LiDAR class schemes never block the points; plugins may ship them (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- Since the old names were dropped (2026-10-26), a class scheme file still
  in the old format stopped the LiDAR import (app and `ohl pointcloud
  import --classes`), and a point cloud that had stored one stopped the
  whole project from opening. Now a scheme that cannot be read is not
  used: the import goes on with the standard classes (ASPRS) and says so;
  a cloud whose stored scheme no longer reads opens with the standard
  classes, said in the load log. The points keep their class numbers;
  a scheme chosen later (Class colours) names and colours them.
- Plugins may ship class schemes as files (`[[class-scheme]] file = …` in
  the manifest, inside the plugin's folder), offered as **From a plugin**
  in the LiDAR import and in Class colours.

**Another project into this one: towers in both, cables by id (owner, 2026-10-27)**

Found when combining several exports of neighbouring lines that share
junction towers and cables: every project-plugin import names its wire
file alike, so a second import's wire file "differed" and was left out
(its new cables missing) or kept both (the same cable id twice: the wire
library refused to load, and then the structure types were not found
either); towers in two exports came in twice or replaced each other.

- **A tower in both is kept once, as the project's** (its id, position,
  orientation and type), and its sets are asked for one by one
  (`ohl_io::import_into::SharedTower`, `SetChoice`; key
  `tower:<imported id>:set:<n>`): a set only in the import is **added**
  (default) or left out (its imported sections and jumpers with it); a
  set in both within the tolerance (the wire points in still air, world
  coordinates, so towers turned differently compare right) is the same
  attachment; a set in both at other places: **keep the project's**
  (default; the imported sections hang on it), **take the imported
  one** (replaces the project's wire point and strings of that set), or
  **add it under a new number** (a free number; the imported sections
  follow). A set added brings the imported wire point and the strings
  above it up to the structure points as the tower's own items (labels
  unique on the tower, string directions turned into the project
  tower's axes; a project point at the same place used). The imported
  tower is taken in effect (resolved with the import's own files). Its
  type file is not added when only towers in both use it. The window
  lists one line per tower, opened to its sets.
- **The same id further than the tolerance is another structure**,
  without asking: an id of its own (`T1-2`), a note with the distance;
  its type comes with it, under a new id and file when the project's
  type file of that name, or its type of that id, is another.
- Programs number alignment points, sections, jumpers and alignments
  alike in every file: **the same id elsewhere** (an alignment point
  beyond the tolerance, a section or jumper over other structures, an
  alignment of another route) is another object, kept apart under an id
  of its own (`sec1-2`), counted in a note. Before, an alignment point,
  structure, section or jumper of the same id was always a duplicate,
  kept as the project's by default: the import lost it. An alignment
  point at the same place alike but for its id is the same.
- **Cables by id, one of each in the project** (owner, the same day):
  the import's wire files are read cable by cable; one the project has
  with the same data is left out; a new one is added **to the project's
  wire file** (the first by name when it has several, said in a note),
  never as a second file of the same name; one of the project's ids with
  other data is a duplicate (`cable:<id>`): keep the project's (default)
  or the imported one under a new id (`<id>-2`, added likewise; the
  imported sections and jumpers name it). A project without a wire file
  gets the import's as it is. A cable the wire library would refuse
  (seen: a cable whose area exceeds its diameter's circle by rounding)
  is left out with a note, so the library keeps loading.
- **Structure type files by type id**; a type file whose name is taken
  by another type is added under a name of its own (`<id>.ohls`)
  without asking (keeping the project's would leave the imported
  structures' type missing). **Every structure's type must be in a type
  file of the project after the import**: the plan lists any that would
  not be (`ImportPlan::missing_types`), in the window before Import and
  on the command line. *Keep both* of a type file now gives the type a
  new id when the project has its id (two files of one id did not
  load).
- The window plans with the project line as stored (before: the line as
  resolved, so typed structures were written back merged with their
  types) and with the project's structure, insulator and wire files.
- **Command line**: `ohl project import-into FILE --into PROJECT.ohl
  --user U --plugin DIR [--option K=V] [--choose KEY=keep|imported|both]
  [--choose tower:T:set:N=add|leave|keep|imported|new] [--route
  ID=existing|new|ROUTE] [--tolerance M] [--dry-run]` prints the plan and
  writes it as one change; it says whether the wire library loads.
- Tests on synthetic data only (the example line split at its junction
  tower: a set only in the import, the same, at another place with each
  choice, a tower of the same id far away with its type, cables alike,
  new and differing, type files); the real exports were checked locally
  only.

**Plugins may suggest wire colours (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- The owner asked for a utility's wire colour table (by owner, voltage,
  frequency and phase) to come from its plugin. Plugins could not set or
  suggest colours: a new optional export `wire-colours` (extension point
  `wire-colours`), additive to interface version 0.3 like
  `sheet-templates` (plugins built before are unchanged). The host sends
  one group per circuit, phase and system with what the line knows (the
  system's owner, number, voltage, frequency, AC/DC) and the plugin's own
  column values; the plugin returns a colour or none per group.
- Applied only when asked (Line › Sections › Wire colours from a
  plugin…): shown first, for the sections without a colour of their own
  (default) or every section, written as the sections' own colours in one
  command. Nothing is coloured behind the user's back, and a project
  opened without the plugin keeps its colours.

**A plugin held below its asked limits says so when it fails (owner report, 2026-10-27)**

- Since the security review (2026-10-26, M6) a WebAssembly plugin whose
  manifest asks for more time or memory runs with the defaults (5 s,
  256 MiB) until the user allows it in the plugin manager. A large file
  through a project plugin then ran out of memory and failed as a bare
  "wasm `unreachable`" trap, which did not say what to do. Every plugin
  call that fails (trap or time limit) while the plugin is held below its
  manifest's `[limits]` now starts its error with the advice to allow it
  in the plugin manager. The limits themselves are unchanged.
- The command line `ohl` did not read what the user allowed (only the
  applications did), so a project plugin asking for more memory always
  failed there, even when allowed. It now reads the same shared plugin
  settings (the applications' data folder, found without the window
  library; a test keeps the folder equal to the applications').

**Version 0.0.2: the macOS download holds only the two apps (owner, 2026-10-27)**

- The v0.0.1 disk image also carried the command line, the examples,
  the licence and a read-me beside the apps. The owner wants the
  Applications folder kept clean: from 0.0.2 the disk image holds only
  OHL-Design, OHL-Structure and the Applications shortcut (the licence is
  inside each app). The `ohl` command line and the example line are a
  separate, optional download on the same release page.
- The repository's releases are immutable, so v0.0.1 stays as it was
  published and the slim build is released as v0.0.2 (workspace version
  0.0.2; the export samples carry the new version).

## 2026-10-26

**Performance review: long tables draw the rows in view (owner, 2026-10-26; items 6 and 7)**

- Display only; the results are unchanged. Redone on the tables as the
  UI reviews left them (units in the headers, numbers right-aligned, the
  value fields' look, the not-a-number usage first): the first version
  (on an older base) could not be merged.
- OHL-Structure: the load table (thousands of rows on a large tower,
  each copied every frame), the Members results (sorted every frame) and
  the Members and Joints sheets were laid out whole every frame. They
  now draw only the rows in view (`rows::Table`: one row height, the
  table taking the room of all its rows in its scroll area, the columns
  kept at their widest cell so far so they do not jump while
  scrolling); the load table reads its rows in place (no copy); the
  Members results are sorted once per run and case shown (the same
  order, `usage_order`: a usage that is not a number first). A member or
  joint picked elsewhere (the 3D view) is still brought into view: by
  its place in the table.
- OHL-Design: the lists of the wire tension, string and internal
  clearance checks, the zone findings, the vegetation spans and the bill
  of materials draw only the rows in view (`rows_in_view::Table`, its own
  copy of the helper; each list's spacing, headers and click-anywhere
  rows kept), so every row is listed (the lists' 5000-row cap is gone;
  the CSV export was always whole). The Tables page sorts on each row's
  cell and its number worked out once, not twice per comparison (the
  same order). Not done: keeping the Tables page's rows between frames
  (solved values arrive from background solves under the same model
  revision; it needs a count of solved cases first).
- Tests: the Members sheet of `type-02` draws its first member and not
  its last until that is picked, then the last and not the first; a
  5000-row list draws fewer than 30 rows and scrolls to row 4000.
- Measured (bench-fast profile, M1 Max under a load of about 20 from
  other builds, one whole harness frame, example `type-02`: 178 members,
  46 joints): Members sheet 1.4–1.6 ms → 0.35–0.6 ms, Joints sheet
  0.9–1.4 ms → 0.45–0.5 ms. A large lattice's frame no longer grows with
  its rows.

**Performance review: the time limits read a shared clock (owner, 2026-10-26)**

- The performance review of 2026-10-26 (owner-approved fixes, speed only:
  the results the same bit for bit) found the time budgets reading the
  system clock on every iteration of every catenary element solve.
- A run (`ohl_core::budget::Run`) now reads no clock without a time
  limit, and with one reads a shared counter that a background thread
  (`ohl-budget-clock`, parked while no timed run is alive) keeps from the
  clock once a millisecond: a time limit is noticed within about a
  millisecond (the tick and the thread's waking), early or late. The
  iterations, the iteration limit and the cancel token are exact; no
  iterate depends on the clock. The catenary element's 10 s backstop is
  gone (it could never trip before its 100 iterations); the enclosing
  wire solve keeps its time limit and cancel token. An iteration limit
  hit by an untimed run says no time ("stopped after reaching the limit
  of 100 iterations").
- Measured (M1 Max, shared with two other builds: load 60–100 on 10
  cores, so CPU time is the measure; invented 60-span line, 131 wind
  steps): the 131 solves 48.7–49.1 s CPU before, 46.9–48.3 s after
  (2–4 %); the synthetic example's solves (every calculation, every
  case, one core) 8.6 s before, 8.1 s after (6 %); again on a quiet
  machine, 7.0 s → 6.75 s (3.5 %). Less than the review estimated from
  its profile (half of the samples in the clock): here the clock reads
  cost a few per cent. Same results: the solves and the zone reports of
  both lines the same bit for bit (`{:?}` dumps compared).

**Performance review: the point checks pass far pieces over (owner, 2026-10-26)**

- With wind steps a point was tested against every state's piece of
  every span near it (the review: 33 µs a point with 131 states).
- The vertical clearance now has the lower bound the radial has: from
  the piece's height range (the bundle's lowest and highest
  subconductor, the slice's rise, the allowance; less 1 µm for the
  rounding of the point found on the wire), a piece that can neither
  give a smaller clearance nor one below the requirement is passed
  over before the exact work.
- The zone check's wire index keeps a cell's pieces in blocks by span
  (`WireSet::grouped`: a span's pieces in every wind state together),
  with the block's bounds: a point beyond the reach of a whole block
  (radial: the block's box less its largest radius and allowance;
  vertical: outside its plan box widened by the zone's width, or above
  its height bound) passes it over at once. Each piece of it would have
  been passed over by the same test, so nothing found changes, per wire
  either (a point beyond the reach is never recorded).
- Measured (CPU time, 60 spans, 131 wind states, 10⁵ points; the index
  built included): vertical 3.4 s → 1.8 s, radial 4.3 s → 3.0 s. Same
  results: the zone reports the same bit for bit; a test checks the
  grouped index against the reference check.
- Merged with the vertical clearance measured on the slope (r / cos β,
  physics review the same day): both bounds measure the bundle's extent
  and the allowance vertically too (the piece's own factor, or the
  block's steepest piece's), so they stay below the exact gap.

**Old names no longer read (owner, 2026-10-26; roadmap U12)**

Before the first release (v0.0.1) the compatibility paths for the names of
before 2026-10-18 are gone: the programs `ols`, `ols-cad` and
`ols-structure`; `import ols` (python/ols); `ols-plugin.toml` manifests
(only `ohl-plugin.toml` is read; the hint for sdk 0.2 plugins went with
it, they are refused as any other version); the `ols` file extensions
(`.ols`, `.ols.json`, `.olsw`, `.olss`, `.olsslc`, `-clearances.olsr`…)
and format ids (`ols-…`, OLS XML's namespace and `ols-line`, the
`ols-xml` importer id); `ols://` invitations; `OLS_BUILD_ID`,
`OLS_STRUCTURE_APP` and every other `OLS_…` variable (`ohl_core::env`
reads only `OHL_…`). `ohl_core::files` lost `legacy_name`, `is_format`,
`open_extensions`, `exists_by_either_name` and the `LEGACY_…` constants;
the tests of the old names (`ohl-cli` `older_names`, `legacy_name`,
`tests/data/before-ohl`) went, and the version-2 line files of
`ohl-line` (`tests/data/*-v2.ohl.json`) carry the new id (their version
is what they test). Kept on purpose, being on-disk or protocol names
rather than readers of old files: the table `ols_meta`, ALPN `ols/2`, the
storage ids `OLS CAD` / `OLS Structure`, the window storage keys
`ols-structure-…`, the web client's `ols.…` browser storage keys, the
ADRs (history). The owner's machine holds no files of the old names, so
no migration. No calculation changed (`ohl validate benchmarks`: 186
passed).

**A Roles page (owner, 2026-10-26)**

What a viewer, a designer and an admin may do is one table in the session
crate (`ROLE_ABILITIES`, each ability with its least role, plus a sentence
per role), shown by a new page **Roles** (View) with the user's own role
marked, and in the server guide. A test tries a sample of its rows against
the session's checks (the role below refused, the least one allowed).

The owner approved the same review for OHL-Design as for OHL-Structure:
both programs look and behave alike, each with its own code (OHL-Design
and OHL-Structure do not depend on each other: `style.rs` and
`notices.rs` copied and adapted, no shared crate). No calculation, file
format or engine changed; every model edit is still one command (undo);
the UI settings below are the window's, kept between runs, not the
project's.

- **Quick bar**: Undo ⟲, Redo ⟳, Save all 💾, Fit views ⛶ and Check wire
